Putin used ideological vocabulary more than twice as often in 2026 as in 2019, while his use of economic terms remained largely static. Among Moscow’s security partners, ideological language held roughly steady between 2023 and 2026, while references to trade, energy and investment doubled. Egypt’s emphasis changed little. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi used ideological terms as often as Putin in 2019, but by 2026 Putin used them 75% more often than Sisi. African leaders outside the core group of eight security partners plus Egypt and Ethiopia used ideological terms 25% less frequently between 2023 and 2026, while the use of pragmatic vocabulary rose by more than a third. Some countries are scaling back their cooperation with Russia amid limited economic returns and tensions over the war in Ukraine. For example, in 2026, South Africa sent its foreign ministry’s director-general and Nigeria a junior foreign minister , replacing the presidents who attended in 2019. Their business programme speaker counts fell from 14 to five and from seven to three, respectively. An opening for Europe Insights from confidential conversations between ECFR’s Africa programme and African policymakers suggest that the continent’s governments and leaders appreciate a more pragmatic approach from European partners. This involves Europeans acknowledging the legacy of European colonialism in Africa, but also realising that in a fragmented global order Africa has options to choose from. Europe would benefit from identifying where Russian political actors are working at cross-purposes and leveraging this fragmentation in diplomatic negotiations with African partners. For example, the former Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin welcomed the Niger coup in 2023, while Russia’s foreign ministry backed ECOWAS in restoring constitutional order. In the CAR, his son Pavel Prigozhin has held on to Wagner’s operations despite the Russian defence ministry’s efforts to absorb them. As Moscow gives its bureaucratic players a bigger role in Africa, such tensions are likely to grow. The Russia-Africa Action Plan for 2027-2029 contains 236 measures, including joint drone, fertiliser and vaccine production, and cooperation between the African Union and the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organisation. But these priorities, and Russia’s bilateral agreements with African countries, can undermine one another: Rosatom requires deep cooperation with Accra to develop the planned nuclear power plant in Ghana, for example, but Russia’s coercive recruitment of Ghanaians for its war against Ukraine risks eroding bilateral trust. Even Mahama, who praised Moscow’s support for Africa’s anti-colonial struggles, has challenged Putin over the practice . Where Moscow’s competing interests undermine its summit promises, Europe can build trust by backing projects that African partners themselves prioritise. An example is the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), for which the EU provided technical and financial support. Despite facing some difficulties, the AfCFTA highlights where European and African strategic interests align—and where Europeans can help Africans reach their objectives, without setting the terms. Europeans also need to understand that, for African partners, pursuing a narrative in which Europe “counters” other actors such as Russia may not land well. Although Africa has considerable growth and market potential, the continent does not want to be approached as an international bargaining field. European governments should instead sharpen their own offer and advance investments in areas such as education and training, technology and engineering. Forums such as the AU-EU Senior Officials Meeting in Addis Ababa are essential for Europe to stay aligned with African priorities, while the participation of high-level European leaders, such as German president Frank-Walter Steinmeier at the upcoming German-African Business Summit in Ghana, signals how seriously they take cooperation. * African partners are not going to wait for European countries to take more responsibility in their approach to economic and trade negotiations. Europeans must ground any partnerships with African countries in reliability—a quality that Russian cooperation has yet to achieve. Both Europe and Africa share a strong belief in multilateralism, political dialogue and collective action. This dialogue, if transformed into a pragmatic, well-coordinated approach , would set Europeans apart from the transactional and extractive approaches of other global players. Source

三边会谈 + 气候呼吁 + 间谍事件 Linda_Heyer Thu, 11/19/2026 - 14:46 picture league / Win McNamee/Pool Getty Images AsiaPac via AP Download (pdf - 720.16 KB) MERICS Briefs MERICS China Essentials Nov 19, 2026 11 分钟阅读 三边会谈 + 气候呼吁 + 间谍事件 头条新闻 普京习近平按自己的方式主持峰会，特朗普成为众人瞩目的焦点 美中俄深圳峰会对俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京来说是一次外交胜利，但习近平成为了更大的赢家，他成功主持了一场可能让中国在深圳举办的亚太经合组织峰会黯然失色的会议。对于因俄罗斯近五年的侵略乌克兰战争而被西方孤立的普京来说，这次会议提供了一个轻松的机会来展现一位在国际外交最高层仍然受欢迎的领导人的形象。对习近平来说，中国对两位不可预测的客人的精心舞台管理得到了回报，峰会既没有像莫斯科所希望的那样就乌克兰问题达成“雅尔塔式”协议，也没有像美国总统唐纳德·特朗普所建议的那样让北京参与削减核武器谈判。
根据俄罗斯政府会后发布的联合声明，三位领导人确实同意“就减少核风险和防止核扩散进行对话”，但这不应损害北京的既定立场，即美国和俄罗斯必须在中国加入任何谈判之前大幅削减其更庞大的核武库。习近平、普京和特朗普还承诺改革联合国，并同意增加石油产量。也许对维护基于规则的国际秩序的西方国家来说最痛苦的是，该声明还表示，国家官员的豁免权是“根本性的”，国际刑事法院不得滥用其权力，该法院于 2023 年对普京发出了逮捕令。后一点将加剧欧洲的担忧，即美国总统在几个问题上与北京和莫斯科更加一致。但乌克兰的未来并未出现在官方结论中，这一事实使欧洲免于陷入更糟糕的境地。在莫斯科本身提高了对三边会议的期望后，普京似乎急于挽回乌克兰问题上缺乏进展的面子，并强调他已与习近平和特朗普分别讨论了这场战争。深圳的情况也没有暗示平等国家的新“G3”。在他们第 50 次面对面会面时，习近平再次称普京为“老朋友”，但没有像接待特朗普那样到机场接待他。
周四，习近平与特朗普的双边会晤和午餐会持续了很长时间，以至于普京不得不等待三边会议开始。“最重要的事情可能是三边会议最终举行了。习近平让普京得到了他所寻求的关注，同时为特朗普保留了红地毯待遇。通过这样做，他成功地举办了一场可能有风险的会议。”  伊娃·塞沃特 (Eva Seiwert)，MERICS 高级分析师 更多相关主题：为什么习近平可能有自己的理由避免美俄中峰会 – MERICS 伊娃·塞沃特 (Eva Seiwert) 的评论 媒体报道和来源：中国外交部（CN）：习近平会见俄罗斯总统普京 BBC：普京称俄罗斯、美国和中国对全球和平负有“共同责任” 路透社：直播：特朗普、习近平和普京举行了前所未有的三边会谈，重点关注乌克兰和核武器METRIX 1,042,590,000,000 这是中国2026年前10个月的贸易顺差，以美元计算。顺差突破1万亿美元三月

Trilateral talks + Climate call-out + Espionage affair Linda_Heyer Thu, 11/19/2026 - 14:46 picture alliance / Win McNamee/Pool Getty Images AsiaPac via AP Download (pdf - 720.16 KB) MERICS Briefs MERICS China Essentials Nov 19, 2026 11 min read Trilateral talks + Climate call-out + Espionage affair Top story Putin gets the spotlight and Trump the red carpet as Xi runs the summit on his terms The US-China-Russia summit in Shenzhen was a diplomatic win for Russian President Vladimir Putin, but Xi Jinping emerged as the bigger winner, successfully managing a meeting that risked overshadowing the APEC summit China was hosting in the same city. For Putin, isolated by the West over Russia’s near five-year war of aggression against Ukraine, the meeting offered an easy opportunity to project the image of a leader still welcome at the highest level of international diplomacy. For Xi, China’s careful stage management of two unpredictable guests paid off, with the summit neither producing a “Yalta-style” agreement on Ukraine, as Moscow had favored, nor binding Beijing into nuclear-arms reduction talks, as US President Donald Trump had suggested.  The three leaders did agree to “engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation,” according to a joint statement released by the Russian government after the meeting, but this should not undermine Beijing’s established position that the US and Russia must make substantial reductions to their much larger arsenals before China joins any talks. Xi, Putin and Trump also committed to reforming the UN and agreed to increase oil production. Perhaps most painfully for Western countries that uphold the rules-based international order, the statement also said immunity for state officials was “fundamental” and that the International Criminal Court, which issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023, must not abuse its authority.  This latter point will reinforce European concerns that the US president is more aligned with Beijing and Moscow on several issues. But the fact that the future of Ukraine did not feature in the official conclusions spared Europe from worse. After Moscow itself had raised expectations for the trilateral, Putin appeared keen to save face over this lack of progress on Ukraine, stressing that he had discussed the war separately with Xi and Trump. The optics in Shenzhen also did not suggest a new “G3” of equal countries.  Xi once again called Putin his “old friend” at what was their 50th in-person meeting, but did not receive him at the airport as he did Trump. Xi’s bilateral meeting and lunch with Trump on Thursday ran so long that Putin was left waiting for the trilateral to begin.  "The most significant thing may have been that the trilateral took place at all. Xi gave Putin the spotlight he sought, while reserving the red-carpet treatment for Trump. In doing so, he successfully managed a potentially risky meeting.”  Eva Seiwert , Senior Analyst, MERICS More on the topic: Why Xi may have his own reasons to avert a US-Russia-China summit – MERICS Comment by Eva Seiwert Media coverage and sources: Chinese MFA (CN): 习近平会见俄罗斯总统普京   BBC: Putin says Russia, US, and China share 'joint responsibility' for global peace Reuters: Live: Trump, Xi and Putin hold unprecedented trilateral talks, with Ukraine and nuclear arms in focus METRIX 1,042,590,000,000 This is China’s trade surplus in the first ten months of 2026, in US dollars. The surplus broke the USD 1 trillion mark in October, one month earlier than in 2025, putting it on track to exceed last year’s record annual surplus of USD 1.2 trillion. A surge in foreign demand for electric vehicles, technology and AI-related products has seen exports outpace imports, even though the latter are themselves growing rapidly. Exports of computer parts were up 235 percent, those of semiconductors up 110.8 percent, and those of vehicles up 52.2 percent. (Source: General Administration of Customs )  GRAPHIC OF THE WEEK China exported 41 billion USD more goods to Germany between January and October 2026 than it imported from Europe’s largest economy – almost twice the trade surplus recorded in the same period last year. As the latest issue of the SOAPBOX newsletter on China reported, citing Chinese customs data, this increase accounted for nearly one third of the 69 billion USD increase in China’s trade surplus with the EU as a whole.  China’s surplus with Germany grew almost five times as fast as the 22 percent rise in its surplus with the rest of the EU, which reached USD 270 billion. This highlights Germany’s deep economic ties with China – and its resulting exposure to Chinese competition. As China sells more higher-value products abroad and increasingly sources components domestically, Germany faces a big double squeeze: rising imports and falling exports.  SOAPBOX is a weekly newsletter on EU-China trade relations compiled by Rafael Buendia Jimenez and Ilaria Perla. You can subscribe to the newsletter for free here . TOPICS China uses COP31 to showcase Europe’s dilemma on climate and trade China’s clear position at November’s UN climate change conference in Türkiye stood in stark contrast to Europe’s growing dilemma between its climate ambitions, defensive trade policy toward China and growing reluctance to commit more financing for developing countries dealing with global warming.  Before COP 31, Beijing had emphasized the need to discuss “old issues” of insufficient climate financing and “new challenges” of unilateralism and protectionism, which were harming “collective efforts to address climate change.” But in the end, it was the African Group that proposed putting climate-related trade and climate finance on the agenda. Their contention that Europe’s additional levy on carbon-intensive imports is unfair to Africa reinforced China's argument that European protectionism is undermining global climate cooperation. The EU objected to these proposals, which included the tripling of finance pledges, but did not block the Climate Finance Work Programme – a process to work out how developed countries meet their climate finance obligations to developing nations – as a separate agenda item.  The bloc is under pressure to fill a US-sized financing gap after US President Donald Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement. Domestic opposition to a larger pledge is growing, as the EU is already one of the largest donors worldwide. Europe’s reluctance to step up, together with a lack of high-level European leaders at the conference stands in a stark contrast to China’s dominant cleantech offer to the world.  "The EU faces a dilemma: decarbonization is needed to fight climate change, but Chinese cleantech dominance and exports to the EU are a geoeconomics challenge. As the EU grapples with this, China’s proposed solution – more Chinese cleantech and more climate funding from developed countries – is gaining momentum.” Johanna Krebs , Analyst, MERICS Media coverage and sources : Xinhua (CN): 以“双碳”为牵引加快全面绿色转型——生态环境部介绍我国应对气候变化工作成效 Down to Earth: COP31 Adopts Climate Finance Work Programme Amid Tensions Over Adaptation Funding and Trade Carbon Brief: COP31: Agenda adopted! - Conversations / Policy   Carbon Brief: Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit Euronews: ‘More than just a photo opportunity’: Why are key EU leaders skipping the COP31 Leaders’ Summit? Nvidia’s espionage drama could backfire on Chinese AI ambitions Revelations that the chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy could deal another blow to China’s AI industry, which is already grappling with an economic slowdown and Beijing’s push for labs to switch to less powerful domestic hardware such as chips designed by Huawei. The US government is openly split between advocates of continued commercial engagement and national-security hawks who want to cut off Chinese access to US AI technology. But pressure from lawmakers in Washington for tighter controls is mounting – and Congress could ultimately override any presidential veto of legislation covering foreign trade. China’s AI stocks, already caught in China’s broader market correction, have slumped again. Huang has not just been Nvidia’s guiding light since co-founding the company in 1993, but he also successfully lobbied US officials, including President Donald Trump, over the last two years to relax chip export controls. US lawmakers now want to crack down on smuggling networks that supply China with the most advanced US-designed AI chips and on schemes that give Chinese companies remote cloud access to powerful chips via data centers located in third countries. The Commerce Department will also soon require companies to obtain licenses for advanced semiconductor exports, re-exports and transfers to data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Data centers anywhere in the world will need permission to service Chinese companies.  "China's AI future is deeply tied to policy decisions made in Washington, which the networks and choices of a few tech CEOs can shape in fundamental ways. Huang was one of the most influential advocates of maintaining the flow of US AI chips to China. But the espionage allegations will make that position much harder to defend – and leave China’s AI industry with even fewer options.” Rebecca Arcesati , Head of Program (Co-Lead) Science, Technology and Innovation, MERICS Media coverage and sources: The New York Times: The Fall of Jensen Huang Reuters: US to curb China's access to AI chips as Trump heads to Asia Bloomberg: Nvidia Stops Selling AI chips to China Despite US Approval Xi tightens his grip on local party committees – in good time for a fourth term Xi Jinping’s third term as General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) ends in the second half of 2027, but it looks like he is not going anywhere. The CCP’s Central Committee on November 7, 2026, issued revised regulations on the work of local party committees for the first time since 2015. The new rules are meant to improve decision-making by cadres in provinces, cities and counties to make sure central directives are implemented. Maintaining a strong chain of command from the center down to the local level is of paramount importance to the CCP’s ability to meet its goals – and to securing Xi’s position at the apex of the party, making a fourth term increasingly likely. Xi and the other then 22 members of the Politburo had announced the review of the regulation in March. They require officials to shoulder “political responsibility” for ensuring that the Central Committee’s policies are effectively implemented. Contradicting the leadership’s directives, engaging in local protectionism, pursuing prestige projects designed to demonstrate political achievements and improperly increasing local government hidden debt are expressly forbidden. Local party committee members are subject to “lifelong accountability” for rule violations and decision-making errors. Although permanent responsibility already applies to environmental and certain major administrative decisions, this is a significant extension of the mechanism. "The ideologies of Marx, Lenin and Mao have been removed from the regulations, while Xi’s status as ‘core leader’ has been codified. His latest instructions and speeches are now the first item on the agenda at local party meetings. Xi wants to put cadres’ feet to the fire and make sure they get the job done the way he wants it. He looks like a leader who expects to keep a close eye on them for a while yet.”  Alexander Davey , Analyst, MERICS Media coverage and sources: SCMP: Communist Party lays down the internal discipline law for local leader s Xinhua (CN): 《 中国共产党地方委员会工作条例 》 (Regulations on the Work of Local Committees of the Chinese Communist Party) Communist Party Member Network (CN): 《 中国共产党地方委员会工作条例 (2015) 》 (Archived version of the previous 2015 regulations) Lianhe Zaobao Singapore (CN): Revised work regulations of local party committees bans "vanity" projects and "prestige" projects China successfully targets rich to boost income-tax revenue China appears to be having considerable success in taxing its richer residents more. Revenues from personal income tax surged 90 percent in October 2026 from a year earlier, after tax authorities in July introduced rules requiring Chinese residents to pay tax on assets transferred into offshore trusts and on income generated by them. Taxpayers – mostly the country’s ultra-rich – had until late October to comply, effectively closing a loophole used to protect assets from the Chinese state. Tax revenue linked to offshore trusts reached CNY 160 billion in the first ten months of 2026, which suggests personal income-tax revenue from January to October 2026 is likely to have already exceeded the 2025 full-year total of CNY 1.62 trillion (about EUR 221 billion).  China’s overall tax revenue has been rising over the past year, spurred in particular by securities trading. But with China’s AI bubble deflating and share prices falling, the additional personal income tax revenue from offshore trusts is a welcome boost to state finances. Personal income tax accounts for only a portion of total tax revenue. At 9 percent, it carries less weight than value-added tax, which accounts for 39 percent of revenues, or corporate income tax, which accounts for 23 percent. But the increased flow of revenues from taxing offshore trust assets and income will provide additional fiscal room by offsetting declines in land-tax and consumption-tax revenue.  “The surge in personal income tax takings is the latest sign of China’s push to expand its tax base and strengthen public revenues. The recent focus on taxing offshore trusts, most of which are owned by high-net-worth individuals, also opens up other opportunities. It allows authorities to exercise greater oversight over capital outflows and potentially redistribute wealth more evenly.” Sophia Pradels , Analyst, MERICS Media coverage and sources: Xinhua (CN): 离岸信托收益征税平稳有序推进 (Offshore Trust Income Taxation Is Progressing Smoothly and Orderly) Yicai: China’s Personal Income Tax Haul Nearly Doubles in October on Offshore Trust Windfall Financial Times: China warns of ‘severe’ punishment for offshore trust tax evaders MERICS CHINA DIGEST China's economy falters as factory output, retail sales undershoot expectations (Reuters) Chinese retail sales grew just 0.4% year-on-year in October, down from 1.1% in September, while industrial production growth slowed to 4.8%.  (26/11/16) China's Singles Day sales rise 4.8% to USD 1.78 trillion; AI takes larger role (Reuters) China's Singles Day shopping generated CNY 1.78 trillion in revenues, but annual sales growth slowed to 4.8% from 14.2% in 2025 despite weeks of promotions. title: Alice Huang’s Shady Shanghai Ties to Business and Government
zh_title: 艾丽丝·黄与上海商界和政府的不正当关系
summary: 内容摘要：黄仁勋间谍丑闻核心人物、Megaspeed 前高管 Alice Huang 通过上海金融界建立了自己的商业网络。她与因财务不当行为而受到制裁的所谓丈夫康伟和后来涉嫌欺诈和贿赂的谷国平等人物有联系。报道称，美国情报部门认为她是中华人民共和国情报部门的合作伙伴。根据开源研究，目前尚不清楚 Alice Huang 在国家安全部 (MSS) 中的确切角色是什么
content:
内容摘要：黄仁勋间谍丑闻核心人物、Megaspeed 前高管 Alice Huang 通过上海金融界建立了自己的商业网络。她与因财务不当行为而受到制裁的所谓丈夫康伟和后来涉嫌欺诈和贿赂的谷国平等人物有联系。报道称，美国情报部门认为她是中华人民共和国情报部门的合作伙伴。根据开源研究，目前尚不清楚 Alice Huang 在国家安全部 (MSS) 中的确切角色是什么；然而，当她结识黄仁勋时，她的兴趣和事工的兴趣很可能是一致的。黄和康利用他们的游戏业务扩展到半导体和数据中心，并在此过程中成为 Nvidia 的客户。随后，黄仁勋接管了香港游戏公司第七大道在新加坡的国际子公司第七大道国际，并通过马来西亚子公司购买了英伟达芯片。美国当局怀疑这些芯片随后被转运到中国。皇康网络与中国地方政府建立了联系。持有顾国平旗下斐讯公司股份的上海松江区投资机构，在顾国平的犯罪活动导致斐讯公司倒闭后，将股份出售给其网络中的一家公司。
科技巨头英伟达 (Nvidia) 联合创始人兼首席执行官 (CEO) 黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 垮台的核心人物是一位名叫黄乐 (Huang Le) 的女性，又名 Alice Huang。媒体报道称，黄女士是英伟达在东南亚最大的客户之一、新加坡计算公司 Megaspeed 的前高管，她与黄仁勋有染。 Megaspeed 涉嫌将受美国出口管制限制的 Nvidia 芯片走私到中华人民共和国（PRC）。报道还称，美国情报部门认为黄女士已被中华人民共和国国家安全部 (MSS) 拉拢（《纽约时报》[NYT]，10 月 29 日；《华盛顿邮报》，11 月 15 日）。 [1] 北京很快否认了这些指控，但一些亲美人士认为中国的知识分子则更加持怀疑态度。他们认为当前的丑闻是特朗普政府内部以及特朗普与“深层政府”之间的内讧的结果（腾讯新闻；X/@Wuuesanren；X/@WoodenHarp，11月10日）。一位上海商人在接受采访时也表达了类似的观点，称黄女士的网络采用了复杂的、多层的公司结构来掩盖最终控制者是谁，并称这种策略是“上海滩从同治皇帝时候就玩的东西了”，指的是19世纪下半叶的早期现代化时期（作者访谈，11月10日）。他相信女士。
黄女士的目的只是将芯片走私到中国。黄出身于上海金融界，她与随后被判犯有金融犯罪的人物的关系表明，她的个人资料应该引起更多的危险信号。她的网络以一家投资公司上海和熙投资管理为中心，该公司是由她所谓的恋人、商人康伟创立的（英国《金融时报》，11 月 10 日）。该网络中的其他主要人物包括黄瑜，英国《金融时报》将其描述为黄女士的妹妹；顾国平

Executive Summary: Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the heart of the Jensen Huang spy scandal, built her business network through the world of Shanghai finance. She is linked to figures such as Kang Wei, her alleged husband who has been sanctioned for financial misconduct, and Gu Guoping, who was later implicated in fraud and bribery. Reporting indicates that U.S. intelligence considers her a cooptee of People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence services. It remains unclear what Alice Huang’s exact role was for the Ministry of State Security (MSS) based on open-source research; however, it is likely that her interests and that of the ministry converged around the time when she became acquainted with Jensen Huang. Huang and Kang used their gaming business to expand into semiconductors and data centers, becoming an Nvidia customer in the process. Huang then took over Hong Kong-based gaming company 7Road’s international subsidiary based in Singapore, 7Road International, and purchased Nvidia chips through a Malaysian affiliate. U.S. authorities suspect the chips were then transshipped to the PRC. The Huang-Kang network cultivated ties with local governments in the PRC. The investment arm of Shanghai’s Songjiang District, which owned a stake in Gu Guoping’s Phicomm, sold the stake to a company in their network after Phicomm failed in the wake of Gu’s criminal activity. At the center of the downfall of Jensen Huang, the co-founder and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of technology giant Nvidia, is a woman identified as Huang Le (黄乐), also known as Alice Huang. Media reporting alleges that Ms. Huang, a former executive of one of Nvidia’s largest customers in Southeast Asia, the Singapore-based computing company Megaspeed, had an affair with Jensen Huang. Megaspeed has been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips covered by U.S. export control restrictions into the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Reports have also said that U.S. intelligence considered Ms. Huang to have been coopted by the PRC’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) ( New York Times [NYT] , October 29; Washington Post , November 15).  [1] Beijing has been quick to deny these allegations, but some pro-U.S. Chinese intellectuals are more skeptical. They view the current scandal as a consequence of infighting within the Trump administration and between Trump and the “deep state” ( Tencent News ; X/@Wuyuesanren ; X/@WoodenHarp , November 10). In an interview, a Shanghai businessman expressed a similar view, saying that Ms. Huang’s network used an elaborate, multilayered corporate structure to conceal who ultimately controlled it, calling this tactic “the sort of thing Shanghai has been doing since the time of the Tongzhi Emperor” (上海滩从同治皇帝时候就玩的东西了), referring to the period of early modernization in the second half of the 19th century (Author interview, November 10). He believed Ms. Huang’s purpose was simply to smuggle chips into the PRC. Ms. Huang emerged from the world of Shanghai finance, where her connections to figures who have subsequently been found guilty of financial crime suggest that her profile should have raised more red flags. Her network centered on an investment firm, Hexi Investment Management (上海和熙投资管理), which was founded by one her alleged romantic partners, the businessman Kang Wei (康伟) ( Financial Times , November 10). Other major figures in this network include Huang Yu (黄瑜), whom the Financial Times describes as Ms. Huang’s sister; and Gu Guoping (顾国平), the founder of communications company Phicomm (斐讯技术) ( Financial Times , November 10; Caixin , November 10).  [2] Ms. Huang co-founded Shanghai Yunxi (上海韵禧) in 2016, and Huang Yu took over the following year ( The Time Weekly , November 9). (Source: Author’s research) Gaming Served as Gateway to Data Centers For Ms. Huang, as for Nvidia, the gaming industry provided a route into the compute business. PRC game publishers often set up foreign entities to serve overseas markets, providing a legitimate reason to import graphics processors and expand data center capacity. Huang became involved with 7Road Holdings (第七大道), a Hong Kong-listed game developer, after it had acquired a portfolio of gaming businesses held by an entity wholly owned by her and registered in the British Virgin Islands ( Caizhongshe , November 11). A circular announcing the acquisition identified a company owned by Kang Wei, Ningbo Jingxuan (宁波镜瑄), as a “party acting in concert” (一致行动人) with Ms. Huang. It also listed among the portfolio’s operating entities in the PRC a company previously owned by a subsidiary of Century Huatong (世紀華通), another firm with ties to Kang and Huang ( Hong Kong Exchange , September 25, 2019).  [3] With Ms. Huang now behind the scenes, Yunxi expanded her business network into the semiconductor and data center industries through cooperation with 7Road starting in 2022. A 7Road subsidiary committed renminbi (RMB) 330 million ($49 million) to a limited partnership managed by Yunxi whose sole asset was a 5.29 percent stake in a Shanghai-based semiconductor wafer manufacturer ( Hong Kong Exchange , May 24, 2022). 7Road also expanded into the data center and cloud computing businesses in 2019, offering cloud services for gaming and the possibility of third-party data center services in a cooperation framework ( Hong Kong Exchange , December 30, 2019; Hong Kong Exchange , May 9, 2021). A 7Road subsidiary involved in Huang’s gaming portfolio later became a vehicle for 7Road’s cloud computing business, buying graphics processors and servers ( Hong Kong Exchange , September 25, 2019).  [4] In 2022, it raised RMB 150 million ($24 million at the time) through a sale-and-lease-back of equipment that included 9,800 graphics processors ( Hong Kong Exchange , March 15, 2022). reported control transfers in May-Jul. 2016"}]} Notes [1] A cooptee is an MSS collaborator, whom the ministry uses for operational support—typically in exchange for favors. They can help make introductions, serve as a go-between for the MSS and a source, provide excuses for sources to travel to the PRC, or otherwise assist the MSS in its operations. The MSS may also approach these people because of the access, business, or other ability that they have to support operations ( National Interest , June 11, 2017). [2] In November 2014, CITIC Securities (中信证券) bought a 3.8 percent stake in a technology firm under a stock return swap with Hexi, helping Gu gain control of the listed company ( CSRC , May 12, 2017). Ms. Huang worked in securities financing at CITIC at the time. The deal may have brought her into contact with Kang a year before she joined Hexi ( Hexi Investment , March 17, 2017). [3] In 2014, Hexi subscribed for shares in Century Huatong connected to its acquisitions of Tianyou Software (天游软件) and Wuxi SevenCool (无锡七酷网络). In 2017, Wuxi SevenCool sold the gaming company Hangzhou Shengfeng (杭州盛锋) to Ningbo Jingxuan (宁波镜瑄), whose ultimate controller is Kang (CNINF, March 9, 2014 , March 7, 2017 ). [4] The name of this firm, Shanghai Lingsu (上海凌素), closely resembles another firm within Ms. Huang’s business network, Shanghai Lingsuda (上海领素达), which invests primarily in smart mobility and ride-hailing platforms (see the Interactive Map) ( CAIC , August 16, 2023; Hong Kong Exchange , December 23, 2024). Yunxi also entered the ownership chain of a data center holding company, also based in Shanghai, and in 2025 changed its own registered name to Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing Data Group (上海珑腾智算数据集团) ( Hong Kong Exchange , September 13, 2023; Times Weekly , November 9). In Shanghai business circles, it is common to register a series of companies with names that share the same Chinese characters or use different characters with the same pronunciation. Other businesspeople can then easily tell who actually controls a company from its name alone. [5] Kang had previously used companies he controlled, including Hexi, to take over three major Phicomm shareholding vehicles ( Sina Finance , August 10, 2018). [6] Such data centers under Kang’s control, with refurbishment nearing completion, would very likely use Nvidia chips smuggled into the PRC through Huang’s Megaspeed. [7] The business tactic of offering one’s spouse to another man reaches even much further back. During the Warring States period, Zichu (子楚), a prince of Qin (秦), took an interest in Zhao Ji (赵姬), the consort of the merchant Lu Buwei (吕不韦). Lu, considering how much he had already bet on Zichu to be the next King of Qin, offered Zhao Ji, who was already pregnant, to him. After Zichu became king of Qin, Lu was appointed chancellor and wielded power over the Qin court ( Records of the Grand Historian , accessed November 11). A historical conspiracy theory even held that Qin Shi Huang (秦始皇), first emperor of ancient China, was Lu and Zhao Ji’s son. In the early 2010s, PRC financial media and business books often portrayed Lu Buwei as a merchant who knew how to bet on real power (through whatever means), fueling an interest in him among businessmen of the era (see Fortune China , March 23, 2011). That was precisely when Kang rose to prominence in business. The post Alice Huang’s Shady Shanghai Ties to Business and Government appeared first on Jamestown .

title: Europe and China 2 – The Age of Developing Disillusion
zh_title: 欧洲与中国2——幻灭的时代

这是有关中国与欧洲关系的三部分系列文章中的第二部分。起初，必要性是欧洲商业与中华人民共和国之间伙伴关系之母。在瑞士商学院，电梯制造商辛德勒的例子仍然是一个主题研究。 1979年，这家瑞士公司成为早期与中国的合资伙伴，尽管它与怡和洋行（Jardine Matheson）有联系，怡和洋行是一家与19世纪鸦片贸易有关的香港贸易公司。原因是：中国出现了住房危机。它正在向天空扩展，因为不断增长的人口需要塔楼。该国缺乏尖端技术，不得不到国外采购。最终，这家瑞士公司战胜了日本和美国的竞争对手。政治起了一定作用。瑞士于1950年承认中华人民共和国，是一个中立国。如今，中国拥有庞大的国内电梯行业，并与芬兰通力公司和日本日立公司等建立了合资企业。中国也需要汽车。它与大众汽车达成协议，到 1983 年春天，大众帕萨特的一个版本（更名为桑塔纳）开始在道路上行驶。其棱角分明的风格成为私人交通革命的象征。这些汽车是由上海大众汽车公司（现称为上汽集团）与德国公司和当地投资者的合资企业生产的。如今，上汽集团已成为电动汽车和电池领域的领导者。
在航空领域，空中客车公司开创了合资制造的先河，比美国飞机制造商麦道公司的合资企业更长久，并为欧洲发动机和技术的盈利出口铺平了道路。尽管中国致力于建造自己的商业上可行的民用客机，但这些出口仍然强劲。这些故事体现了欧洲的乐观情绪，这种乐观情绪伴随着中国从 2001 年开始加入世界贸易组织 (WTO)，并推动了本世纪初的贸易交易和外国直接投资。正如香港驻日内瓦代表所说，这是“双赢”。紧张的早期迹象出现在专利和所有权纠纷中。中国官员经常将“技术转让”视为对双方都有利的好事。它成为在某些领域开展业务的条件。跨国公司的国家经理往往主要热衷于扩大在中国的业务，他们会向总部保证他们的中国合作伙伴是值得信赖的。获取最新注册以接收定期电子邮件并随时了解 CEPA 的工作。

This is the second of a three-part series on China’s relationship with Europe. At first, necessity was the mother of partnership between European commerce and the People’s Republic of China. At Swiss business schools, the example of Schindler, the elevator maker, remains a keynote study. In 1979, the Swiss company became an early joint venture partner with China, even though it had ties with Jardine Matheson, the Hong Kong-based trading house associated with the opium trade of the 19 th century. The reason: China had a housing crisis. It was expanding skyward because a growing population required tower blocks. The country lacked sophisticated technology and had to shop abroad. Eventually, the Swiss firm won out over Japanese and American competitors. Politics played a part. Switzerland had recognized the People’s Republic in 1950, and it was a neutral power. Today China has a giant domestic elevator industry of its own plus joint ventures with, among others, Kone of Finland and Hitachi of Japan. China also needed cars. It made a deal with Volkswagen and by the spring of 1983 a version of the VW Passat, renamed the Santana, was plying the roads. Its angular style became a symbol of a revolution in private transport. The cars were manufactured by Shanghai Volkswagen Automotive, today known as SAIC, in a joint venture with the German firm and local investors. Today SAIC is a leader in the field of electric vehicles and batteries.   In aviation, Airbus pioneered joint venture manufacturing, outlasting a venture by the US plane maker McDonnell-Douglas and paving the way for profitable European exports of engines and technology, which remain strong despite China’s drive to build a commercially viable civil airliner of its own. These stories exemplified the optimism in Europe which accompanied China’s membership of the World Trade Organization (WTO) from 2001 and drove trade deals and foreign direct investment through the early years of this century. It was, as the Hong Kong representative in Geneva had said, “win-win.” The early signs of strain emerged in disputes over patents and ownership. Chinese officials regularly spoke of “technology transfer” as a good which would serve both sides. It became a condition of doing business in certain fields. Multinational country managers, often keen primarily to expand their footprint in China, would assure head offices that their Chinese partners could be trusted. Meanwhile, low-cost Chinese manufactured goods poured into European markets under the tariffs agreed on entry to the WTO. Initially confident of their negotiating power as a bloc, the Europeans refrained from resorting to rhetoric about trade wars or dumping. The Chinese export wave, known today as the China Shock, was seen by specialists as a transitional phenomenon that would eliminate itself through the magic of free trade. Today’s leader, Xi Jinping, watched from a critical vantage point as the manufacturing and export boom in China turned a pariah state into an economic powerhouse that had foreign governments, banks and corporations knocking on its door. His fortunes, indeed, advanced with the country’s renaissance. Xi’s career took off in the coastal province of Fujian, which stood at the forefront of China’s export zones. It received a flood of investment from Taiwan, whose manufacturers realized that instead of trying to sell goods into the Chinese market, they should make things cheaply in China to sell to others. This was the trick that turned the world economy inside out. At some point during this period, party elders decided to favor Xi Jinping as a rising official whose consciousness of the value of trade was matched by his cautious disposition. In China, the consensus remained that prosperity and peace were indivisible (which also lowered the risks of any adventure to seize Taiwan). When Xi moved up the hierarchy to vice president in 2008, he visited a slew of European nations as he worked to understand foreign countries and to grow into the top role. He, too, was being auditioned: he met Joe Biden, then also vice president. For all the courtship of Europe, it was the United States which mattered most to China. That is why the financial crisis in the West of 2008 dealt such a blow to Chinese reformers. It broke out in the American credit markets and then spread to Asia. The economic slowdown was the most serious problem the Chinese regime had faced in the new century. Exports collapsed by a fifth, foreign investment slowed, domestic consumption fell, and thousands of factories closed, leaving between 10 and 20 million workers jobless. The blow fell most heavily in the coastal export zones where Xi had made his name and the global trade experiment was at its height. The crisis almost consumed the administration of President Hu Jintao and Prime Minister Wen Jiabao. The technocrats rallied the central bank, raided currency reserves and threw the power of the state behind a $500bn stimulus package that poured funds into high-speed trains and urban infrastructure, reforming the tax system and doling out credit. It was the zenith of pragmatic managerialism in China, but the legacy would be more Communist Party control, a taste for intervention in markets and an iron determination on the part of Xi Jinping that China would never again be subject to the shocks of international capitalism. Facing down America and balancing Chinese economic interests with Europe would be his mission. Michael Sheridan is a veteran British foreign correspondent and is the author of ‘ The Gate to China ’, an acclaimed history of Hong Kong, and ‘ The Red Emperor: Xi Jinping and His New China ’, which is published by Hachette Books and has been translated into a dozen languages, including Ukrainian, Polish, and Japanese. title: Launch Preview: Russian, Chinese, and SpaceX rockets to launch space station missions
zh_title: 发射预览：俄罗斯、中国和 SpaceX 火箭将发射空间站任务
summary: 十枚火箭将于下周发射，其中三枚将访问近地轨道上的两个不同空间站。 Progress MS-36 and CRS NG-25 are expected to deliver supplies to the International Space Station, while Shenzhou 24 is scheduled to launch the next crew to the Chinese Tiangong Space Station, including its first international visitor. Outside of space station flights, Falcon 9 is set to launch a pair of USSF missions from Vandenberg, and China is set to launch a quadruple-header of payloads to orbit.最后，Electron 将发射一颗合成孔径雷达卫星。联盟号2.1b
content:
十枚火箭将于下周发射，其中三枚将访问近地轨道上的两个不同空间站。进步号 MS-36 和 CRS NG-25 预计将向国际空间站运送物资，而神舟二十四号计划将下一批宇航员送入中国天宫空间站，其中包括第一位国际访客。除了空间站飞行之外，猎鹰 9 号还将从范登堡发射两次 USSF 任务，而中国也将向轨道发射四联有效载荷。最后，Electron 将发射一颗合成孔径雷达卫星。联盟号 2.1b |进步 MS-36 11 月 24 日星期二，俄罗斯向国际空间站 (ISS) 发射了进步 MS-36。 Progress MS-36 于世界标准时间 10:13 从哈萨克斯坦拜科努尔航天发射场的 Site 31/6 升空。 Progress MS-36，也被 NASA 称为 Progress 97P，是对国际空间站的补给任务。 Progress 是一艘源自联盟号的航天器，能够携带约 2.5 吨的货物到国际空间站。 Progress MS-36 是 Progress 的第 189 次飞行，于 1978 年首次飞行并与礼炮 6 号空间站对接。 Progress MS-32 从拜科努尔航天发射场升空。 （图片来源：NASA+）联盟 2.1b 是一款三级煤油和液氧运载火箭，源自 R-7 洲际弹道导弹。联盟号 2.1b 可以向低地球轨道 (LEO) 输送高达 8,700 公斤的重量。可以配备可选的第四级 Fregat 或 Volga，用于最终轨道调整。
周二的飞行将是联盟号 2.1b 2026 年的第 10 次飞行，也是整体的第 109 次飞行。 阿丽亚娜 64 |亚马逊狮子座 (LE-04) 在周二的三次发射中的第二次，阿丽亚娜 64 火箭向近地轨道发射了另一批 36 颗亚马逊狮子座卫星。发射窗口于世界标准时间 10:45 开始，并延长至世界标准时间 11:14，阿丽亚娜 6 号在该窗口结束时发射。这次发射是阿丽亚娜 6 号计划进行的 18 次狮子座发射中的第四次。阿丽亚娜 6 是由阿丽亚娜集团为欧洲航天局开发的两级液氢和液氧动力火箭。阿丽亚娜 6 可以配备两个或四个固体火箭助推器来增加升空推力，LE-04 则配备四个。周二的发射是 2026 年阿丽亚娜 6 号的第五次发射任务，也是总共的第十次飞行。阿丽亚娜 64 在 LE-01 任务期间上升（图片来源：ESA/M. Pédoussau） Falcon 9 | USSF-266 在周二的第三次发射中，猎鹰 9 号为美国太空军 (USSF) 发射了一个机密有效载荷。 USSF-266 原定于 11 月 23 日星期一从加利福尼亚州范登堡太空部队基地 (VSFB) 于 11 月 24 日发射升空。 USSF-266 的发射窗口于太平洋标准时间上午 7:55（世界标准时间 15:55）开始，并延长至太平洋标准时间上午 11:55（世界标准时间 19:55），猎鹰 9 号于太平洋标准时间上午 11:08（世界标准时间 19:08）发射。根据空投区，USSF-266 很可能是 USSF 天基机载移动目标指示器计划 (SB-AMTI) 的一部分。 SB-AMTI 是在 Starshield 卫星总线的基础上构建的，而 Starshield 卫星总线本身又源自 Starlink 卫星总线。
助推器 B1081 进行了第 29 次飞行，之前曾飞行过 Crew 7、CRS-29、PACE、Transporter 10 和 13、EarthCARE、NROL-186 和 -48、TRACERS & Others、CSG-3、USSF-153 和 USSF-481。这款特殊助推器是从 SpaceX 目前所有活跃的 Falcon 9 发射台上进行过飞行的少数助推器之一。 B1081 在发射后大约八分钟降落在 SpaceX 的无人机“当然我仍然爱你”在太平洋上。长征2F/G |神舟二十四号周三，中国向天宫空间站发射了下一次载人飞行任务。她

【原文 English Original】
Ten rockets are set to launch over the next week, with three visiting two different space stations in low-Earth orbit. Progress MS-36 and CRS NG-25 are expected to deliver supplies to the International Space Station, while Shenzhou 24 is scheduled to launch the next crew to the Chinese Tiangong Space Station, including its first international visitor. Outside of space station flights, Falcon 9 is set to launch a pair of USSF missions from Vandenberg, and China is set to launch a quadruple-header of payloads to orbit. Lastly, Electron will launch a synthetic aperture radar satellite. Soyuz 2.1b | Progress MS-36 On Tuesday, Nov. 24, Russia launched the Progress MS-36 to the International Space Station (ISS). Progress MS-36 lifted off at 10:13 UTC from Site 31/6 at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan. Progress MS-36, also called Progress 97P by NASA, is a resupply mission to the ISS. Progress is a Soyuz-derived spacecraft capable of carrying around 2.5 tonnes of cargo to the Station. Progress MS-36 served as the 189th flight of Progress, which first flew in 1978 and docked with the Salyut 6 space station. Progress MS-32 lifts off from Baikonur Cosmodrome. (Credit: NASA+) Soyuz 2.1b is a three-stage kerosene-and-liquid-oxygen launch vehicle derived from the R-7 intercontinental ballistic missile. Soyuz 2.1b can deliver up to 8,700 kg to low-Earth orbit (LEO). An optional fourth stage, Fregat or Volga, can be equipped for final orbital adjustments. Tuesday’s flight will be the 10th Soyuz 2.1b flight in 2026 and the 109th overall. Ariane 64 | Amazon Leo (LE-04) The second of three launches on Tuesday saw an Ariane 64 rocket deliver another batch of 36 Amazon Leo satellites to LEO. The launch window opened at 10:45 UTC and extended until 11:14 UTC, with Ariane 6 launching at the end of the window. This launch was the fourth of 18 Leo launches scheduled on Ariane 6. Ariane 6 is a two-stage, liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen-powered rocket developed by ArianeGroup for the European Space Agency. Ariane 6 can be equipped with either two or four solid rocket boosters to augment liftoff thrust, with LE-04 flying with four. Tuesday’s launch was the fifth Ariane 6 mission of 2026, and the 10th flight overall. Ariane 64 ascents during the LE-01 mission (Credit: ESA/M. Pédoussau) Falcon 9 | USSF-266 The third launch on Tuesday saw Falcon 9 launch a classified payload for the United States Space Force (USSF). Originally scheduled for Monday, Nov. 23, USSF-266 launched on Nov. 24 from Vandenberg Space Force Base (VSFB) in California. The launch window for USSF-266 opened at 7:55 AM PST (15:55 UTC) and extended until 11:55 AM PST (19:55 UTC), with Falcon 9 launching at 11:08 AM PST (19:08 UTC). Based on drop zones, USSF-266 is most likely part of the USSF’s Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator Program (SB-AMTI). SB-AMTI is built off of the Starshield satellite bus, which itself is derived from the Starlink satellite bus. Booster B1081 flew its 29th flight after previously flying Crew 7, CRS-29, PACE, Transporter 10 and 13, EarthCARE, NROL-186 and -48, TRACERS & Others, CSG-3, USSF-153, and USSF-481. This particular booster is one of a few boosters to have flown from all of SpaceX’s currently active Falcon 9 pads. B1081 landed on SpaceX’s droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific approximately eight minutes after launch. Chang Zheng 2F/G | Shenzhou 24 On Wednesday, China launched its next crewed mission to its Tiangong Space Station. Shenzhou 24 lifted off from Site 91 at the Jiquan Satellite Launch Complex (JSLC). The launch is currently set for 10 minutes into a 40-minute-long window at 00:18 UTC. The crew was launched aboard a Chang Zheng 2F/G (CZ-2F/G) rocket, which has carried every Chinese crewed mission to date. The three-person crew flew to Tiangong aboard the Shenzhou spacecraft, which borrows many characteristics and designs from Russia’s crewed Soyuz vehicle. Chang Zheng 2F/G with Shenzhou 24 leaves the assembly building. (Credit: CCTV) Shenzhou 24 features a crew of three astronauts, with two Chinese taikonauts, Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, and one Pakistani astronaut, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali. Shenzhou 24 will be Ali’s first spaceflight, and he will spend a short duration aboard Tiangong. This flight marks the first time a non-Chinese astronaut has ever visited Tiangong, which has been in orbit since 2021. The CZ-2F/G is a two-stage, hypergolic rocket equipped with four side boosters that stand 58 m tall. The vehicle is fueled by dinitrogen tetroxide and unsymmetrical dimethyl hydrazine (UDMH), both of which are highly carcinogenic. Shenzhou 24 will be the 18th crewed Chinese flight and the 24th overall in the Shenzhou program. Chang Zheng 2D | Unknown Payload The first of two launches on Thursday features a Chang Zheng 2D (CZ-2D) that will deliver an unknown payload to orbit. This mission is set to liftoff at 09:35 UTC, five minutes into a 22-minute window, from Launch Complex 3 (LC-3) at the Xichang Satellite Launch Center. CZ-2D is a two-stage launch vehicle, with an optional third stage, standing 41 m tall. The rocket is powered by hypergolic fuels and is capable of lofting 3,500 kg to LEO. Thursday’s flight will be the eighth mission of 2026 for CZ-2D, and the 109th overall. Electron | Night Owls Never Sleep Flying from the Mahia Peninsula in New Zealand on Friday, Nov 27, Rocket Lab’s Electron will launch a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite to LEO for Synspective. The mission, named “Night Owls Never Sleep,” is scheduled to liftoff at 00:05 UTC. SAR is used to image the surface of the Earth and can penetrate through cloud layers. Launch 101 coming right up. We're preparing to launch our 101st Electron next week to deploy another StriX Earth-imaging spacecraft for @synspective . The "Night Owls Never Sleep" launch window opens: 1:00 pm NZDT, Nov 27 00:00 UTC, Nov 27 9:00 am JST, Nov 27 7:00 pm… pic.twitter.com/pfblD6s70R — Rocket Lab (@RocketLab) November 20, 2026 Electron is a two-stage, small-lift vehicle capable of delivering up to 300 kg to LEO. The vehicle is fueled by liquid kerosene and liquid oxygen, which powers nine Rutherford engines on the first stage and a single vacuum-optimized Rutherford on the second stage. This mission will serve as Electron’s 22nd mission of 2026 and 101st overall. Chang Zheng 6A | Unknown Payload On Friday, China is set to launch a Chang Zheng 6A (CZ-6A) from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, carrying an unknown payload into orbit. The launch window opens at 12:53 UTC and extends until 13:15 UTC. Currently, liftoff is scheduled for seven minutes into the window at 13:00 UTC. CZ-6A is a two-stage, liquid kerosene-and-liquid-oxygen rocket capable of delivering up to 8,000 kg to LEO. CZ-6A is additionally powered by four solid rocket boosters, which augment first-stage thrust. The vehicle stands 50 m tall with a normal fairing or 52 m tall with an extended fairing. This flight will serve as the 10th CZ-6A mission of 2026 and 29th overall. Chang Zheng 6C | Unknown Payload The last launch of the week from China features a Chang Zheng 6C (CZ-6C) also launching from Taiyuan, delivering an unknown payload to LEO. The launch window opens at 03:46 UTC and extends until 04:15 UTC, with liftoff scheduled for 03:50 UTC, four minutes into the window. CZ-6C is a two-stage, liquid kerosene- and liquid oxygen-powered rocket capable of delivering 4,500 kg to LEO. CZ-6C stands 43 m tall and is considered a single-stick variant of CZ-6A, flying without the solid rocket boosters. Sunday’s launch will be CZ-6C’s second of 2026, and third overall. Falcon 9 | USSF-380 Falcon 9 is set to fly again from VSFB on Sunday, delivering USSF-380 to LEO for the USSF. The launch window opens at 8:39 PM PST on Nov. 28 (04:39 UTC on Nov. 29) and extends until 2:39 AM PST (08:39 UTC, both on Nov. 29). USSF-380 is a classified mission for the USSF but is believed to be part of its Space-Based Sensing and Targeting (SBST) portfolio. SBST is built off of the Starshield satellite bus. The exact number of satellites being launched is unknown but is believed to be similar to that of a typical Starlink mission, based on Falcon 9’s drop zones. Booster B1082 will support this mission on its 27th flight. B1082 has previously supported USSF-62 (WSF-M 1), OneWeb #20, NROL-145, Transporter 18, and 22 Starlink missions. Following stage separation, B1082 will land aboard SpaceX’s droneship Of Course I Still Love You approximately eight minutes after launch. Falcon 9 | CRS NG-25 The final launch of the week will see a Falcon 9 deliver the CRS NG-25 cargo resupply mission to the ISS. CRS NG-25 will launch from Space Launch Complex 40 (SLC-40) at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station (CCSFS) in Florida, with the instantaneous launch window opening on Sunday, Nov 29, at 10:50 AM EST (15:50 UTC). Cygnus XL approaches the ISS for berthing. (Credit: NASA) CRS NG-25 will be the fifth of six planned Cygnus flights aboard Falcon 9, as Northrop Grumman and Firefly Aerospace work to bring their upcoming Antares 330 rocket online in the near future. Additionally, CRS NG-25 will be the third flight of Cygnus XL, which can carry 5,000 kg of cargo to the Station. CRS NG-25’s Cygnus XL is named “ SS James ‘Jim’ Lovell ” after the Apollo 8 and Apollo 13 astronaut who passed away in August 2025. Supporting CRS NG-25 will be booster B1096 on its ninth flight. B1096 has previously supported the Starlink Group 6-87, KF-01, NROL-77, NROL-95, GPS III SV09, CRS-34, CRS-35, and IMAP & Others missions. The booster will return to CCSFS to land at Landing Zone 40 (LZ-40), which is located directly adjacent to SLC-40. Sunday’s recovery attempt will be Falcon 9’s 700th attempted recovery, of which 682 have been successful. CRS NG-25 will serve as the 125th Falcon 9 mission and the 281st orbital launch attempt worldwide in 2026. (Lead Image: Falcon 9 launches from Florida. title: Observations from Taiwan’s Education Frontline amid Cognitive Warfare
zh_title: 认知战中台湾教育前线的观察
summary: 下载整期 PDF 作为全球台湾研究所致力于促进声音多元化的一部分，全球台湾简报偶尔会发表台湾年轻人撰写的文章。我们很高兴以一名高中生的视角来阐述年轻人在复杂的互联网信息环境中所面临的挑战，以及台湾学校关于公民教育的持续争论。台湾面临着一些严重的威胁，不仅来自直接的军事力量，还来自我在同龄人中经常看到的自我挫败的态度。虽然在国外
content:
下载整期 PDF 作为全球台湾研究所致力于促进声音多元化的一部分，全球台湾简报偶尔会发表台湾年轻人撰写的文章。我们很高兴以一名高中生的视角来阐述年轻人在复杂的互联网信息环境中所面临的挑战，以及台湾学校关于公民教育的持续争论。台湾面临着一些严重的威胁，不仅来自直接的军事力量，还来自我在同龄人中经常看到的自我挫败的态度。尽管外国观察家警告两岸可能发生冲突，但年轻人流行的社交媒体平台上却充斥着“战争不会爆发”、“台湾无论如何也不会赢”或“谁统治我们并不重要”等言论。但这些言论并不代表台湾大多数青年群体的声音，也不应被视为整个一代人放弃的证据。然而，随着对民主的冷漠成为日常谈话的一部分，它产生了一种值得关注的脆弱性。问题的出现并不仅仅是因为一些学生对政治了解太少。事实上，我们许多人在与我们学校设计的环境截然不同的信息环境中遭遇政治。公民教育仍然主要通过教科书、考试和课堂讲座进行。
然而，政治叙事现在通过短视频、影响者、模因和推荐算法传达给我们。如果学校以中立的名义避免讨论有争议的问题，学生将不会变得政治中立：相反，他们会去其他地方学习政治。当政治通过信息传播时 中国社交媒体平台已成为台湾信息环境的主要组成部分。 TikTok、抖音和 Rednote 等平台模糊了娱乐和政治影响力之间的界限。事实上，可能影响台湾人的内容并不总是需要采用明显的宣传。现代天际线、高铁、传统文化、美食、乡村生活、普通家庭的视频都能让中国成为一个熟悉而有吸引力的国家。政治信息可以通过娱乐视频传播，而台湾年轻人可能根本不认为这些是政治信息。这不是一个边缘问题。事实上，Doublethink Lab 2025 年的一项研究（使用台湾传播调查的数据）发现，50.73% 的高中生使用 TikTok。研究人员还采访了 16 名 15 岁至 18 岁的台湾用户，发现政治视频有时会意外地出现在社交媒体群组中，尤其是在 2024 年总统选举前后。尽管如此，研究人员发现，大多数青少年仍然对中华人民共和国政府持负面看法，反对统一。
因此，声称使用中国平台会让台湾青少年“亲中国”的说法过于简单化。更重要的问题可能是台湾年轻人在这些平台上遇到什么样的政治信息，以及他们如何理解这些信息。当我们超越屏幕上出现的内容时，这种担忧变得更加清晰。 2025 年对 700 名台湾 Z 世代成员进行的一项同行评审研究发现，更频繁地使用中国社交媒体平台（包括 TikTok、Rednote 和微博）与对两岸事务的政治了解较低有关

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF As part of the Global Taiwan Institute’s commitment to promoting a diversity of voices, the Global Taiwan Brief occasionally publishes articles written by Taiwanese youth. We are pleased to present this perspective from a high school student about the challenges young people face in navigating a complex internet information environment, and continuing debates over civic education in Taiwan’s schools. Taiwan faces several serious threats, not only from direct military forces, but also from a self-defeating attitude that I see frequently in people of my age. While foreign observers warn of the possibility of a cross-Strait conflict, social media platforms popular among young people are filled with claims that “War won’t break out,” “Taiwan could never win anyway,” or “It doesn’t matter who governs us.” Nonetheless, these statements do not represent the voice of the majority of youth groups in Taiwan, and they should not be seen as proof that the entire generation has given up. However, as indifference toward democracy becomes a part of everyday conversation, it creates a sort of vulnerability that deserves attention. The problem arises not simply because some students know too little about politics. In fact, many of us encounter politics in an information environment very different from the one for which our schools were designed. Civic education still largely proceeds through textbooks, exams, and classroom lectures. Political narratives, however, now reach us through short videos, influencers, memes, and recommendation algorithms. If schools avoid discussing controversial issues in the name of neutrality, students will not become politically neutral: instead, they will go somewhere else to learn about politics. When Politics Spreads Through the Feed Chinese social media platforms have become a major part of Taiwan’s information environment. Platforms such as TikTok, Douyin, and Rednote blur the line between entertainment and political influence. Indeed, content that may impact Taiwanese does not always have to employ obvious propaganda. Videos of modern skylines , high-speed rail, traditional culture, food, rural life, or ordinary families can render China a familiar and attractive country. Political messages can then spread through entertainment videos, and Taiwanese youth may not perceive these as political messages at all. This is not a marginal issue. In fact, a 2025 Doublethink Lab study —using data from the Taiwan Communication Survey—found that 50.73 percent of high-school students used TikTok. Researchers also interviewed sixteen Taiwanese users aged fifteen to eighteen and discovered that political videos had sometimes appeared unexpectedly in social media groups, especially around the 2024 presidential election. Nonetheless, the researchers found that most of these teenagers still had negative views of the PRC government and opposed unification. It is thus an oversimplification to claim that using Chinese platforms makes Taiwanese teenagers “pro-China.” The more important question may be what kind of political information Taiwanese youth encounter on those platforms, and how they understand it. That concern becomes clearer when we look beyond what appears on the screen. A 2025 peer-reviewed study of 700 members of Taiwan’s Generation Z found that more frequent use of Chinese social media platforms—including TikTok, Rednote, and Weibo—was associated with lower political knowledge about cross-Strait affairs, and a weaker ability to tell the different usages of language between China and Taiwan. Greater use of Chinese social media was also linked to a decreased ability to identify People’s Republic of China (PRC) disinformation. This does not necessarily mean that young people are being “brainwashed.” The problem may be more subtle. If people have less knowledge about an issue, it becomes harder for them to judge whether the information they see is reliable in the first place. The numbers from another Doublethink Lab nationwide survey make this picture even more complicated. Among 2,612 Taiwanese respondents aged fifteen and above, the majority of both frequent and non-frequent TikTok users rejected the idea of giving up democracy for cross-Strait peace. Yet there was still a difference between the frequent and non-frequent users. The study found that 30.3 percent of frequent users were willing to accept giving up democracy for peace, compared with 23.4 percent of non-frequent users. Frequent users were also more likely to believe that unification with China might not significantly change everyday life in Taiwan. These numbers do not prove that TikTok caused these attitudes. But they do suggest that cognitive influence does not have to make young Taiwanese actively admire Beijing. Sometimes, it may simply make the differences between democratic and authoritarian systems feel less important, or make resistance seem less worthwhile. What “Politics Out of Schools” Originally Meant If political influence increasingly reaches students through their phones, then Taiwan must also ask what role schools should play. Here, our democratic history creates an ironic situation. During the authoritarian period of Taiwan, politics was not absent from Taiwanese campuses. Rather, politics was deeply intertwined with education. Historical records show that Kuomintang (國民黨) organizations, the China Youth Corps (中國青年救國團), military instructors, and state security agencies were involved in monitoring and managing university campuses. In 1986 and 1987, as Taiwan moved toward democratization, students involved in the “Freedom of Love” movement (自由之愛運動) at National Taiwan University demanded freedom of speech, university autonomy, and reform of the University Act (大學法) , as well as the removal of party organizations, the Youth Corps, and military instructors from campuses. This history matters because the original democratic demand was not that students should stop discussing politics. Instead, it was that the party-state should stop controlling political life in schools. Indeed, demands for political institutions to leave campuses appeared alongside demands for greater freedom of expression. Removing political control is not the same as removing political discussion. Taiwan’s legal framework still reflects this distinction. Article 6 of the Educational Fundamental Act (教育基本法) requires education to follow a principle of neutrality and prohibits schools from either campaigning for particular political organizations, or forcing teachers and students to participate in political activities. The restriction is directed at the institution, not at the student. Taiwan democratized its schools by making institutions politically neutral, not by requiring students to be politically silent. Image: A teacher and students at Baozhong Junior High School in Yunlin County, Taiwan (December 2019). Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) From Political Neutrality to Political Silence Yet in practice, the memory of authoritarian political indoctrination may have encouraged a broader habit of avoiding controversial politics in school. The idea that “politics should not enter schools” (政治不入校園) can be interpreted not only as a warning against party control, but also as a reason for teachers to avoid politically sensitive issues. This is different from the original purpose of educational neutrality, which was to protect students from forced ideology, rather than to stop them from discussing political life. The same tension can also be seen inside schools. A National Academy for Educational Research (國家教育研究院) survey of high-school history teachers found broad support for teaching transitional justice, but more than 60 percent of teachers worried that such teaching could be influenced by partisan viewpoints. Among teachers who did not design additional lessons on transitional justice, fear of being accused of partisan indoctrination was the second most common reason— after lack of class time. This does not mean that teachers do not want to discuss politics. Rather, it shows how easily civic education can be confused with political indoctrination, even in a democratic society. The tension is especially clear because Taiwan’s curriculum has moved in the opposite direction. The 108 Curriculum (108課綱) included transitional justice in high-school history, and education researchers have also recommended using multiple historical perspectives to encourage discussion and reflection. Formally, schools are therefore expected to help students think critically about history, understand different perspectives, and reflect on democratic values. At the same time, teachers may still worry about being accused of taking sides. As many of my classmates have noticed, political issues can therefore become exam facts that we memorize for answer sheets, but quickly escape our memory. Civics exists as an academic subject, but politics does not always become part of students’ real lives. History can feel distant from our own identities, while democratic rights become background conditions that we assume will always exist. When students then hear “If there’s war, just surrender” or “It doesn’t matter who is in charge,” they may understand the danger of war without having seriously thought about what political change could mean for freedom of speech, elections, personal rights, or the rule of law. This is where the role of the classroom becomes important. Schools should not tell students which party to support or what position to take on cross-Strait relations. Instead, they should give students a place to ask questions, test claims, compare evidence, and discuss difficult issues. Research using data from 3,953 Taiwanese students in the International Civic and Citizenship Education Study found that an open classroom climate for discussion was associated with stronger civic knowledge and expected electoral participation. In other words, students do not become better citizens simply because disagreement is kept out of the classroom. They need opportunities to learn how to disagree while still respecting evidence, rights, and one another. Rebuilding Civic Resilience Taiwan can learn from the experiences of other democracies. Austria has included political education in its formal education system and emphasizes that controversial issues should also be presented as controversial in the classroom, while avoiding political indoctrination. Finland , meanwhile, treats media literacy as an important part of education and integrates it across subjects, helping students understand information, media, and misleading content. These two examples show that political education and media literacy do not have to mean telling students what to believe. Instead, they can help students understand political issues, recognize different viewpoints, and evaluate the information they receive. Taiwan has also begun to recognize this need. In 2025, the Ministry of Education (教育部) announced plans to develop teaching materials on understanding China, including cross-Strait relations, national identity, and possible risks. By July 2025 , thirteen teaching materials had undergone initial review, and were still being revised and supplemented. However, as a student on the front line of Taiwan’s education system, I was barely aware of this plan. Most of the teachers and classmates I asked had not heard about it either. Even if the material is still under review, students should be able to understand what is being prepared, why it is needed, and when they may actually have the chance to use it. A policy cannot have much effect on students if the students themselves barely possess awareness of it. For this reason, the Taiwanese government should expedite the development of these materials and simultaneously seek to raise awareness among students and teachers regarding what changes are underway. However, teaching materials alone may not be enough. Taiwan should also consider adding more opportunities for civic education and discussion in schools, especially on topics such as cross-Strait relations, democracy, media literacy, and how political information affects our daily lives. Taiwan does not need to copy either Austria or Finland’s models exactly. Its own history provides the more important lesson. Taiwan’s democratization movement fought to remove one-party control from schools so that thought could become freer. The purpose of that effort was never to create classrooms in which politics could not be discussed. Modern cognitive warfare makes this distinction urgent. Algorithms do not respect the principle of “politics out of schools.” They enter teenagers’ lives every day, deciding what we see. If schools in democracies respond by remaining silent, they leave the most politically consequential part of students’ education to systems designed not to educate citizens, but to maximize attention. The challenge, then, is not to bring partisan politics back into schools. It is to bring democratic politics back into civic education. Students should understand how Taiwan’s freedoms were won, how authoritarian systems differ from democratic ones, how algorithms can shape political perception, and how to examine claims without automatically accepting or rejecting them because of party labels. Taiwan’s psychological defense will not be built by teaching young people what to think. It will be built by giving them the knowledge and habits necessary to decide what is worth defending for themselves. The main point: As political information increasingly reaches Taiwanese youth through social media, schools’ reluctance to discuss controversial issues may leave students more vulnerable to misleading narratives and cognitive influence. Political neutrality should not mean political silence. Instead, Taiwan’s civic education should encourage open discussion, critical thinking, and media literacy, allowing students to develop their own informed judgments about democracy and the challenges it faces. The post Observations from Taiwan’s Education Frontline amid Cognitive Warfare appeared first on Global Taiwan Institute .

The Death of Logic and Sanity in Silicon Valley bbert@hudson.org Tue, 11/24/2026 - 13:49 SVG Commentary Nov 24, 2026 Washington Times The Death of Logic and Sanity in Silicon Valley Our technology giants are helping China challenge American supremacy   Miles Yu Senior Fellow and Director, China Center Miles Yu Commentary Caption The headquarters of NVIDIA in the Silicon Valley, Santa Clara, California, November 6, 2025. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents Share to Twitter Twitter Share to Facebook Facebook Share to LinkedIn LinkedIn Share to E-mail E-mail Print Print Something has gone terribly wrong in Silicon Valley . The industry that made America the world’s technological superpower has produced executives whose commercial ambitions increasingly collide with national security. Their dealings with communist China expose an astonishing paradox: American technology companies help China catch up with the United States, then warn that China is catching up, and finally use that warning to demand permission to sell China even more advanced technology. No one is more vocal in advancing this lunacy than Nvidia’s now-reinstated CEO Jensen Huang . Mr. Huang’s latest scandal has been sensationalized, focusing on his illicit relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed . Yet the bigger issue is Mr. Huang’s absurd ideas about China and its artificial intelligence industry. Mr. Huang has repeatedly argued that China is catching up with or even winning the AI race, that American export controls are futile or “the dumbest thing we’ve ever done” and that restricting advanced chip sales to China will ultimately undermine American technological leadership. He says those resisting his ideas — whom he labels “ China hawks” — are unpatriotic and un-American. These arguments are intellectually vacuous, characteristically arrogant, strategically reckless and remarkably self-seeking for Nvidia’s commercial interests. Worse, they reflect a broader Silicon Valley mentality that confuses corporate profits with America’s national interest. Consider the contradictions. If China is winning the AI race, why are Chinese companies so desperate for Nvidia’s advanced chips? If American AI models such as Claude and ChatGPT are losing their technological edge, why do China’s top AI firms, such as Kimi and Alibaba, seek to extract their capabilities through large-scale distillation? If American export controls are futile, why does Beijing devote extraordinary resources to circumventing them? How can supplying America’s foremost strategic adversary with the technologies underpinning American supremacy possibly strengthen America’s competitive advantage? Mr. Huang’s vicious dismissal of “ China hawks” as wearing a “badge of shame” makes defending American technological superiority sound disgraceful whenever it interferes with corporate profits. His arguments collapse under the absurdity of their own logic. In fact, this is Silicon Valley’s self-fulfilling prophecy, a circular argument that converts the consequences of its own commercial decisions into justification for repeating them. China’s technological progress remains critically dependent on American semiconductor designs, advanced AI chips, computing infrastructure and technical expertise. Without access to these capabilities, Beijing would face far greater obstacles in developing cutting-edge AI. China’s scientists and engineers are capable, and its government invests enormous resources in innovation. Yet its relentless pursuit of American technology reveals how much its technological ambitions still depend on foreign breakthroughs. Mr. Huang’s corporate behavior is also in question. Multiple reports indicate that Megaspeed has purchased more than $4.8 billion in advanced Nvidia AI chips since June 2024 and has erased the records of these transactions from its books. American authorities have investigated suspected diversion through Southeast Asian intermediaries. Reports have also raised questions about Ms. Huang’s suspected ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter reportedly contacted Commerce Department investigators, citing clearance from Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler, regarding the Megaspeed investigation. Nvidia denies wrongdoing and says it stopped supplying Megaspeed in June 2025, but recent reports dispute the denial. Congress and law enforcement should investigate the Megaspeed affair, examine possible interference with export-control enforcement and close loopholes involving third-country intermediaries, remote computing access and sensitive technology licensing. Proven violations deserve serious penalties. Nvidia is hardly alone. Consider Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, Mr. Huang’s distant cousin. In 2016, under her leadership, AMD entered into a technology-licensing agreement worth approximately $293 million, plus royalties, with Chinese partners affiliated with the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The arrangement transferred valuable x86-compatible processor technology and first-generation Zen intellectual property into China’s industrial ecosystem. The available record indicates the transaction was lawful. Its strategic wisdom deserves scrutiny. Why should American companies help develop China’s indigenous computing capabilities and then warn Americans about the technological challenge they helped create? Cisco provides another cautionary example. Falun Gong practitioners accused the company of supplying technologies that helped China’s Golden Shield surveillance system identify and track religious believers. Cisco disputed the allegations, and this year the U.S. Supreme Court dismissed the lawsuit, holding that the Alien Tort Statute does not allow aiding-and-abetting liability against corporations. Yet the controversy illustrates the risks of American technology becoming entangled with authoritarian surveillance. The Chinese Communist Party systematically mobilizes civilian technology for military modernization, intelligence operations and political control. U.S. executives advocating greater access to technology for China must confront these strategic consequences. America’s technological supremacy rests on decades of innovation, enormous investment and hard-won expertise. Allowing these advantages to strengthen its principal strategic adversary threatens the foundations of American security. Silicon Valley has perfected a vicious cycle of strategic folly: Sell advanced American technology to China , often knowingly and furtively through a third, surrogate country such as Singapore. Watch Beijing close the gap. Warn Americans that China is catching up. Declare export controls futile. Demand permission to sell even more advanced technology to China . Repeat. Each turn enriches Silicon Valley , strengthens Beijing and erodes America’s technological supremacy. The closer China gets, the louder the alarm — and the louder the alarm, the greater the pressure to sell China more. Eventually, the prophecy fulfills itself: Silicon Valley helps China catch up, warns America that China is catching up, and uses that warning to help China catch up even faster, until America loses the race its own technology giants helped China win. In other words, Silicon Valley has lost its mind. In explaining his support for Mr. Huang’s reinstatement, President Trump has said Mr. Huang has learned his lessons. Let us hope these lessons learned will help Silicon Valley regain its sanity. Read in the Washington Times. Enjoyed this analysis? 黄仁勋 Megaspeed 丑闻对欧洲意味着什么？乍一看，情况并不多：欧洲人将继续购买英伟达芯片。但仔细观察就会发现，连锁反应将对跨大西洋关系以及欧洲与北京日益紧张的关系产生影响。荷兰及其明星芯片制造商 ASML 看起来尤其容易受到影响。黄也许是华盛顿最有影响力的中国鸽派。他几乎单枪匹马地说服唐纳德·特朗普总统及其内阁采取宽松的方式执行拜登时代对英伟达芯片的出口管制，这激怒了两党鹰派。他的影响力减弱，再加上有关通过新加坡向中国非法走私芯片规模的新揭露，意味着鹰派再次得势。美国商务部已经采取行动，禁止中国人工智能公司使用海外数据中心。三项法案似乎将被纳入《国防授权法》，以进一步打击中国使用美国芯片。其中之一——MATCH法案——针对的是中国的芯片制造工具供应。荷兰公司 ASML 是这些工具的全球主要制造商。在美国制裁的威胁下，它将被迫遵守其美国竞争对手目前面临的相同限制。
包括荷兰王室在内的欧洲和荷兰外交官已经游说反对 MATCH 法案，该法案看起来不太可能成为法律——直到 Megaspeed 丑闻爆发。 实际上，该法案将禁止 ASML 向中国销售新的芯片制造机器（中国约占该公司年收入的五分之一），并禁止 ASML 履行为该国现有机器提供服务的合同义务。获取最新注册以定期接收带宽电子邮件并随时了解 CEPA 的工作情况。电子邮件提交 Δ document.getElementById( "ak_js_9" ).setAttribute( "value", ( new Date() ).getTime() ); gform.initializeOnLoaded( function() {jQuery('#gform_ajax_frame_9').on('load',function(){var content = jQuery(this).contents().find('*').html();var is_postback =contents.indexOf('GF_AJAX_POSTBACK') >= 0;if(!is_postback){return;}var form_content = jQuery(this).contents().find('#gform_wrapper_9');var is_confirmation = jQuery(this).contents().find('#gform_confirmation_wrapper_9').length > 0;var is_redirect =contents.indexOf('gformRedirect(){') >= 0;var is_form = form_content.length > 0 && is_redirect &&！

What does the Jensen Huang Megaspeed scandal mean for Europe? At first glance, not much: Europeans will keep buying Nvidia chips. But a closer look shows that the ripple effects will have consequences for transatlantic relations and for Europe’s increasingly tense relationship with Beijing. The Netherlands and its star chip machine manufacturer, ASML, look particularly vulnerable. Huang was perhaps Washington’s most influential China dove. He almost single-handedly persuaded President Donald Trump and his cabinet to take a lax approach to enforcing Biden-era export controls on Nvidia chips, to the fury of hawks on both sides of the aisle. His diminished influence, coupled with fresh revelations around the extent of illegal chip smuggling to China via Singapore, means that the hawks once again have the wind in their sails. The Department of Commerce has already moved to  block  Chinese AI companies from using overseas data centers. Three bills look  set  to be rolled into the National Defense Authorization Act that would further crack down on China’s use of US chips.  One of them — the MATCH Act — takes aim at China’s supply of chipmaking tools. Dutch company ASML is the major global manufacturer of these tools. It would be forced to comply with the same restrictions currently faced by its US competitors, under threat of US sanctions.  European and Dutch diplomats, including the Dutch Royal Family, have already  lobbied  against the MATCH Act, which looked unlikely to pass into law — until the Megaspeed scandal broke. In effect, the Act would ban ASML from selling new chipmaking machines to China, which accounts for around a  fifth  of the company’s annual revenue, and from fulfilling its contractual obligations to service existing machines already in the country.  Get the Latest Sign up to receive regular Bandwidth emails and stay informed about CEPA's work. Even if the MATCH Act passes, the White House will have discretion over how aggressively the legislation is applied. President Trump has tried to shield Nvidia and maintain good relations with Chinese President Xi Jinping. That gives Washington leeway to decline to enforce its toughest provisions — but still leaves ASML vulnerable to shifting political priorities or a future, more hawkish administration. If the US ultimately forces ASML to cut off servicing to Chinese companies, the Netherlands — and Europe — could find themselves exposed to Chinese retaliation. When Beijing  imposed  export controls on rare earths in 2025 in response to US trade actions, it ensured European companies were also caught in the crossfire. Beijing would likely not hesitate to make an example out of the Netherlands in order to discourage other countries from allying too closely with Washington. The MATCH Act is being discussed just as Europe itself is in the middle of executing a major hawkish turn on China, driven by the latter’s industrial overcapacities and supply chain dominance. Whereas the EU was unwilling to take a strong stance on China during Trump’s first term — when administration officials pressed European countries to remove Huawei telecoms equipment — and under former President Joseph Biden, the bloc is now developing powerful new trade instruments directed against Beijing. Despite this shift, Europe’s China policy remains fundamentally defensive. European capitals do not share Washington’s interest in undermining China’s AI sector. In fact, the EU benefits from Chinese competition to closed-source US frontier labs. Europe’s telecoms incumbents are resisting ripping out Huawei from their networks,  arguing  that the exclusion of Chinese suppliers would be  costly  and leave them dependent on expensive local vendors. US China hawks should think twice before trying to strong-arm Europe into mirroring US China policy. Such a move would likely backfire by galvanizing anti-US and pro-China figures in Europe. There is a deal to be done. For their part, EU countries need to follow through on the tough talk and deliver on China de-risking, with concrete measures such as improving coordination and closing gaps in EU and national licensing of chipmaking components. If Washington sees Europe acting of its own accord, it can formally take the threat of sanctions off the table. In the end, controls that allies adopt through their own volition are likely to prove more durable than those imposed on them by ultimatum.
