content:
科罗拉多州东部的许多农民和牧场主对人工智能感到好奇，但他们没有当地精通技术的人来向他们展示如何使用人工智能。薛“爱丽丝”董已将此作为她的工作。董是 IEEE 高级会员，也是科罗拉多州立大学推广部门（CSU 的外展部门）的推广区域专家。她在洛根县工作，为科罗拉多州东北角的 10 个县农业区提供服务。她的工作是将大学研究转化为对居住在那里的人们的实际帮助。薛“爱丽丝”董 雇主 科罗拉多州立大学洛根县推广 职称 推广区域专家 会员等级 高级会员 母校内蒙古师范大学，位于呼和浩特；北京师范大学；纽约州立大学环境科学与林业学院，位于锡拉丘兹；科罗拉多州立大学全球分校 她构建了人工智能驱动的农业旅游聊天机器人 (AgriTourismAI.com)，帮助农民和牧场主启动和经营“农业旅游”业务。农业旅游是指农民向游客开放他们的土地以进行娱乐、教育或购物活动。常见的例子包括采摘自己的果园、如何种植蔬菜的课程以及手工产品的销售。董还举办研讨会，向农民和牧场主展示如何使用人工智能工具来帮助发展和管理他们的业务。她说她将自己视为大学和农村之间的纽带。 “我们（推广专家）充当桥梁，”她说。
“我们将校园与我们服务的农村社区联系起来。”许多农民和牧场主年龄较大，通常没有接受过技术培训。他们的子孙常常离开农场到城市工作，或者无法教他们新工具。如果没有帮助，人工智能的好处可能会与农民失之交臂。 Dong 的研讨会为他们提供了一条出路。Dong 凭借她的 AgriPivot AI Agent 入围 2026 年 GenAI for Good Challenge 决赛。该挑战赛由 IEEE Humanarian Technologies 和联合国国际电信联盟组织，她的项目是从 79 个国家的 318 个团队中选出的。她还获得了国家推广技术社区 (NETC) 颁发的 2026 年创新奖，以及国家社区发展推广专业人员协会 (NACDEP) 颁发的 2025 年国家和西部地区教育技术奖。作为首席研究员或联合首席研究员，她获得了七项竞争性资助，总额超过 25 万美元，其中包括由农业部国家食品和农业研究所支持的资金。董出生于北京，从小就热爱设计和解决问题。她的父母都是医生。小时候，她喜欢画新的、有创意的东西。她说，素描可以让她用图片解决脑海中的问题，并将它们作为实际设计写在纸上。这个习惯逐渐成为她与周围环境相处的一种方式。
她说：“我一直热衷于创造一些有形的东西来解决现实世界中的问题。”她并不将自己的人生方向归功于任何一位导师。相反，她说她所有的老师都帮助她为她的职业生涯奠定了基础。她就读于位于呼和浩特的内蒙古师范大学，这是一所培训教师的机构。 2013 年，她在那里获得了两个学士学位——一个是地理科学学士学位，另一个是教育学士学位。然后，她获得了课程和教学硕士学位

【原文 English Original】
Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job. Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension , CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there. Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan County Title Extension regional specialist Member grade Senior member Alma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products. Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business. She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside. “We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.” Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in. Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and the U.N.’s International Telecommunication Union , and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC) , and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP). She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture . An early love of design and problem-solving Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors. As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs. That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings. “I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says. She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career. She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University , in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education. She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016. That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry , in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020. From outreach to extension work After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College , in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator. She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water. She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain , helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park. In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County ’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns. She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds. Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System , a nationwide network run by land-grant universities , schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states. The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture , managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties. The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program , which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship. Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person. She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says. “We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says. Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI . The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly. How her AI chatbot helps farmers and ranchers In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree , in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global . She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python , a popular programming language . It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT ’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it. The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download. Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.” Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk. One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch , in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases . Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication. Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) . The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing. She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude , and Gemini . She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp ., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp ., Colorado Startup Week , and Boulder Startup Week . And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel. Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools , she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use. She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says. Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.” How IEEE membership supports her career Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology . She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group . IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences. IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.” She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE. Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone. “They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

韩国已成为全球人工智能（AI）热潮的最大受益者之一。其半导体产业快速增长，提高了出口、企业利润和国民收入。但这种成功也带来了严重的脆弱性：韩国的主导产业越强大，经济对单一全球技术周期的依赖就越大。
半导体行业正在快速增长。 2026年前10个月，韩国商品出口同比猛增60%以上，达到9300亿美元，其中半导体占比近43%。芯片需求强劲和出口价格上涨帮助推动经济增长远超预期。国际货币基金组织将韩国 2026 年经济增长预期从 1 月份的 1.9% 上调至上个月的 3.3%，并于上周上调至 3.9%。
这不仅仅是普通的半导体好转。对人工智能数据中心的大规模投资刺激了对先进高带宽内存（HBM）芯片的需求，韩国制造商在这方面拥有强大的竞争地位。对人工智能采用持续进展的预期表明，对计算能力和内存的需求可能会持续增长多年。
但韩国半导体繁荣的好处分配不均。芯片制造需要大量资本投资，但创造的新就业机会相对较少。较高的利润和工资集中在单一行业的龙头企业和熟练工人身上，而小企业、服务提供商和低技能工人则被抛在后面。尽管半导体员工和供应商支出的增加可以支持当地消费，但芯片行业与其他经济领域之间的差距仍然很大。
此外，韩国对半导体的依赖增加了其面对全球冲击的脆弱性 — — 特别是人工智能行业泡沫破灭的情况。该技术的变革潜力并不能保证当前的投资热潮将不间断地持续下去。 《经济学人》估计，到 2030 年，人工智能需要产生 3 万亿美元的年收入，才能证明对数据中心和计算基础设施的计划投资是合理的。
美国的政治和监管压力可能会加大经济衰退的可能性。在最近的中期选举中，由于担心数据中心的电力消耗、用水以及对当地社区的影响，美国选民以压倒性多数支持对数据中心实施更多限制，甚至彻底暂停。
更高的融资成本、令人失望的收入、更严格的监管或基础设施建设的延误可能会减缓美国的人工智能投资，在芯片制造商扩大产能之际削弱对韩国半导体的需求。短缺很快就会变成供应过剩和价格下跌。韩国央行预计经济放缓

South Korea has emerged as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Its semiconductor industry is growing rapidly, lifting exports, corporate profits, and national income. But this success makes for an acute vulnerability: the stronger South Korea’s leading industry becomes, the more dependent the economy is on a single global technology cycle.
The semiconductor industry is growing at a rapid pace. In the first 10 months of 2026, South Korea’s merchandise exports surged by more than 60 percent year on year, reaching $930 billion, with semiconductors accounting for nearly 43 percent of the total. Stronger chip demand and rising export prices have helped push economic growth well above expectations. The International Monetary Fund raised its 2026 growth forecast for South Korea from 1.9 percent in January to 3.3 percent last month, and to 3.9 percent last week.
This is more than an ordinary semiconductor upturn. Massive investments in AI data centers have fueled demand for advanced high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, where South Korean manufacturers hold a strong competitive position. Expectations of continued progress on AI adoption suggest that demand for computing power and memory could continue expanding for years.
But the benefits of South Korea’s semiconductor boom are unevenly distributed. Chip manufacturing requires enormous capital investment but generates relatively few new jobs. Higher profits and wages are concentrated among leading firms and skilled workers in a single industry, leaving small businesses, service providers, and lower-skill workers behind. Although increased spending by semiconductor employees and suppliers can support local consumption, the gap between the chip industry and the rest of the economy remains substantial.
Moreover, South Korea’s dependence on semiconductors increases its vulnerability to global shocks – in particular, anything resembling a bubble collapse in the AI sector. The technology’s transformative potential does not guarantee that the current investment boom will continue uninterrupted. The Economist estimated that AI would need to generate $3 trillion in annual revenue by 2030 to justify the planned investments in data centers and computing infrastructure.
Political and regulatory pressures in the United States could make a downturn more likely. In the recent midterm elections, U.S. voters overwhelmingly backed more restrictions and even outright moratoria on data centers, over concerns about data centers’ electricity consumption, water use, and effects on local communities.
Higher financing costs, disappointing revenues, tighter regulations, or delays in infrastructure construction could slow AI investment in the United States, weakening demand for South Korean semiconductors at a time when chipmakers are expanding capacity. Shortages would quickly turn into oversupply and falling prices. The Bank of Korea estimates that a slowdown in U.S. investment in 2027 could cause South Korean semiconductor exports to fall by up to $100 billion below earlier projections, reducing South Korea’s GDP growth by approximately 0.4 percentage points. Falling corporate earnings could depress stock prices, weaken business investment, and reduce corporate tax revenues.
An AI bust could also threaten global financial stability. With tech firms increasingly reliant on private credit and entangled in complex circular-financing arrangements, a downturn could have far-reaching financial consequences. The U.S. Federal Reserve’s latest Financial Stability Report identified AI as the most frequently cited financial stability risk among surveyed market participants.
Trade tensions are another challenge. South Korea’s merchandise trade surplus reached nearly $295 billion in the first ten months of 2026, more than five times the level recorded a year earlier. That includes a $102 billion surplus with the United States. Already, U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has used tariffs to wrest concessions from countries running surpluses with the United States, including South Korea. The possibility of another round of U.S. demands cannot be dismissed.
South Korea also risks being collateral damage in the China-U.S. rivalry. South Korea’s semiconductor industry sits at the intersection of U.S. technology, Taiwanese advanced manufacturing, and Chinese electronics production. Samsung and SK Hynix operate manufacturing facilities in China, which is a major destination for Korean chip exports.
But Washington has long sought to restrict China’s access to advanced technologies. The recent scandal involving Nvidia’s ousted-then-reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, has added momentum to efforts to tighten export controls. New U.S. restrictions have already forced Samsung and TSMC to suspend some chip shipments to Chinese customers. Further restrictions could disrupt not only South Korean chip sales to China, but also the maintenance and upgrading of factories there.
In the longer term, such restrictions will motivate China to develop its own advanced chip sector. Already, Chinese memory producers are expanding their capacity and investing in more sophisticated chips. Though South Korea’s firms retain a considerable technological advantage today, particularly in advanced memory, China might gradually catch up, thanks to its large domestic market and substantial government support. As a result, South Korea could face heightened competition in conventional memory and, eventually, higher-value products.
To remain competitive, South Korea must continue to strengthen its semiconductor leadership. Innovation in HBM, advanced packaging, chip design, and manufacturing equipment requires skilled workers, reliable infrastructure, and predictable regulation. But strengthening an already dominant industry cannot, by itself, resolve the economy’s structural vulnerabilities. The larger task is translating semiconductor success into productivity gains across the economy.
To this end, South Korea must lead on AI adoption, particularly in manufacturing, health care, finance, logistics, and other services. Progress on this front will require investment in human capital, greater labor-market flexibility, support for entrepreneurship, and regulatory reform. The fiscal windfall from the semiconductor boom should support productive long-term investments and strengthen fiscal buffers, rather than finance permanent spending commitments.
South Korea’s semiconductor boom is an extraordinary opportunity, not a guarantee of long-term prosperity. The true measure of its success will be whether the South Korean economy continues to thrive when the chip cycle eventually turns.

title: Copper price erases Nvidia rebound as investors steer clear of metals
zh_title: 由于投资者避开金属，铜价抹去了英伟达的反弹
summary: 周二，铜价回吐了周一人工智能推动的全部涨幅，因为在最近的人工智能暴跌期间抛售金属的投资者几乎没有回归的兴趣，而且交易员不断将美国库存转移到中国。纽约早盘交易中，Comex 12 月交割的铜价下跌 3.5%，至每磅 5.437 美元（每吨 11,985 美元）。该水平的结算价将是 3 月 24 日以来的最低水平。该合约周一结算价为 5.634 美元，上涨 2.7%，但远低于 Nvidia 恢复黄仁勋担任首席执行官后创下的盘中高点 5.787 美元。周二的下跌使铜价比历史纪录低 21%
content:
周二，铜价回吐了周一人工智能推动的全部涨幅，因为在最近的人工智能暴跌期间抛售金属的投资者几乎没有回归的兴趣，而且交易员不断将美国库存转移到中国。纽约早盘交易中，Comex 12 月交割的铜价下跌 3.5%，至每磅 5.437 美元（每吨 11,985 美元）。该水平的结算价将是 3 月 24 日以来的最低水平。该合约周一结算价为 5.634 美元，上涨 2.7%，但远低于 Nvidia 恢复黄仁勋担任首席执行官后创下的盘中高点 5.787 美元。周二的下跌使铜价比 9 月 9 日创纪录的 6.889 美元下跌 21%，从技术上讲，这是一个熊市。该金属今年已下跌 3%，11 月份则下跌 16%。据路透社报道，伦敦金属交易所三个月期铜在官方交易中下跌 3.5%，至每吨 12,054 美元，此前曾一度跌破 12,000 美元。周一该股上涨了 5.3%。 11 月 12 日黄仁勋辞职后，在人工智能暴跌期间出售大宗商品的投资者并没有急着回来。 Panmure Liberum 分析师汤姆·普莱斯 (Tom Price) 对路透表示：“这些投资者并未完全重新投入事件发生前的头寸，其中包括大宗商品敞口。”他表示，许多人认为铜的波动性太大，正在削减大宗商品的投资，以专注于人工智能股票。杭州成联实业的基本金属交易员Aces Zhou告诉彭博社：“现在市场做空铜的原因有多种。”
他表示，除了人工智能的叙述之外，随着铜离开美国，贸易流开始逆转，支撑铜价两年上涨的因素正在瓦解。加息和强势美元加剧了阻力。据彭博社报道，市场完全预计美联储 12 月会议将上涨 25 个基点，这将是今年的第二次会议，而根据 BMO 资本市场的数据，美元指数处于 2025 年 3 月以来的最高水平。美国金属运往中国 现货市场依然紧张，但资金流已经压倒了市场，BMO分析师上周参加上海亚洲铜周后写道。可见的交易所库存仅能满足大约两天的消费量，而进口到中国的洋山溢价在一个月内从每吨不到 100 美元攀升至 500 美元左右。 BMO表示，这些溢价，加上纽约和伦敦价格之间的差距缩小，促使贸易商预订了估计3万吨至10万吨的美国阴极，以便直接运往中国。这些金属存放在美国西海岸的交易所仓库外，大约需要两周时间才能抵达。 BMO表示，发货量的重要性不在于吨位，而在于它们所发出的信号：贸易商正在对一项关税决定失去信心，该决定将使美国库存与世界其他地区隔绝。
中国业内人士预计唐纳德·特朗普总统将放弃对精炼铜征收关税的计划，而西方参与者仍倾向于征收关税。 BMO预计，抛售将持续下去，直到华盛顿方面发出关税意向或价格大幅下跌以影响供应，可能在每吨10,000美元至11,000美元的范围内。该银行表示，托克的成本曲线显示，通过溶剂萃取和电解提取生产的铜中约有 10% 已经亏损，亏损额约为 13,000 美元。 BMO 坚持其中期结构性看涨观点。冶炼厂就 2027 年处理费进行了挤压谈判，矿工向冶炼厂支付的精矿加工费用仍然相差甚远。安托法加斯塔报道

【原文 English Original】
Copper gave back all of Monday’s artificial intelligence-fuelled gains on Tuesday as investors who dumped metals during the recent AI rout showed little appetite to return, and traders kept moving US stockpiles to China. Comex copper for December delivery fell 3.5% to $5.437 a pound ($11,985 a tonne) in morning trade in New York. A settlement at that level would be the lowest since March 24. The contract settled at $5.634 on Monday, up 2.7% but well off the session high of $5.787 reached after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive. Tuesday’s drop leaves copper 21% below its record settlement of $6.889 on September 9, technically a bear market. The metal is now down 3% this year and 16% in November. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 3.5% at $12,054 a tonne in official trading after briefly ducking below $12,000, Reuters reports. It had jumped as much as 5.3% on Monday. Investors who sold commodities during the AI rout that followed Huang’s resignation on November 12 are not rushing back. “These investors are not fully reengaging the positions they had pre-event, which includes commodity exposure,” Panmure Liberum analyst Tom Price told Reuters. Many have decided copper is too volatile and are cutting commodity exposure to concentrate on AI stocks, he said. “There are now multiple reasons for the market to short copper,” Aces Zhou, a base metals trader at Hangzhou Chenglian Industrial, told Bloomberg. Beyond the AI narrative, he said, trade flows are starting to reverse as copper leaves the United States, and the factors that supported the metal’s two-year rally are unravelling. Rate hikes and a strong dollar add to the headwinds. Markets are fully pricing a quarter-point increase at the Federal Reserve’s December meeting, which would be the second this year, Bloomberg reports, and the dollar index is at its highest since March 2025, according to BMO Capital Markets. US metal heads to China The physical market remains tight, but financial flows have overpowered it, BMO’s analysts wrote after attending Asia Copper Week in Shanghai last week. Visible exchange inventories cover only about two days of consumption, and the Yangshan premium for imports into China climbed from under $100 a tonne to around $500 in a month. Those premiums, together with a narrowing gap between New York and London prices, have prompted traders to book an estimated 30,000 to 100,000 tonnes of US cathode for direct shipment to China, BMO said. The metal, held outside exchange warehouses on the US west coast, takes about two weeks to arrive. The shipments matter less for the tonnage than for what they signal, BMO said: that traders are losing confidence in a tariff decision that would keep US stockpiles sealed off from the rest of the world. Chinese industry players expect President Donald Trump to drop plans for duties on refined copper, while Western participants still lean towards a tariff being imposed. BMO expects the selloff to extend until Washington signals its tariff intentions or prices fall far enough to hit supply, potentially in the $10,000 to $11,000 a tonne range. Trafigura’s cost curve shows about 10% of copper produced by solvent extraction and electrowinning is already losing money at around $13,000, the bank said. BMO stands by its structurally bullish medium-term view. Smelters squeezed Talks on 2027 treatment charges, the fees miners pay smelters to process concentrate, remain far apart. Antofagasta has reportedly offered around minus $200 a tonne, while China’s Tongling has signalled about minus $80 could be acceptable, according to BMO. This year’s benchmark was set at zero, already a record low, and BMO estimates some Chinese smelters break even on a cash basis at around minus $90. A deeply negative 2027 benchmark could speed up output cuts, especially as falling sulphuric acid prices erode by-product income. Mine supply remains tight. Global copper mine production fell 1% year on year in September and is down 1% over the first nine months of 2026, the International Copper Study Group said in its latest monthly bulletin. Output from Chile slumped 15% and Peru 9% in the month, more than offsetting gains in Indonesia, China and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Refined demand fell 2% from a year earlier, slightly more than supply, leaving the refined market in deficit for the month, though it remains in surplus for the year to date. Miners give back gains Copper stocks reversed much of Monday’s rally. Freeport-McMoRan fell 5% at the New York open, cutting its market value to $68 billion, and Southern Copper lost 4% to $117 billion. Teck Resources dropped 4% to $25 billion, while BHP slipped 2% to $174 billion and Rio Tinto 2% to $125 billion. The five New York-listed heavyweights shed about $15 billion in the first minutes of trading, after adding more than $25 billion on Monday. In London, Antofagasta dropped 7%, Anglo American almost 6% and Glencore 4%, while Poland’s KGHM fell 7%. In Toronto, First Quantum Minerals lost 6%, Lundin Mining and Hudbay Minerals 5% each and Ivanhoe Mines 4%. BHP this week outlined plans to spend up to $17.4 billion to roughly double copper output in South Australia to about 650,000 tonnes a year by 2040, with a final investment decision expected in the first half of 2027. First Quantum Minerals and Panama opened formal negotiations on Monday over the Cobre Panama mine, shut since 2023, after the company accepted the government’s five conditions for talks, including recognition that Panama owns the mineral resource. Trader Trafigura has taken full control of the $260 million La Farola copper-gold project in Chile, buying the remaining 50% of owner Minera Altair as it moves from trading concentrate into mine development. In Santiago, the price slump is threatening President José Antonio Kast’s budget plans , as copper accounts for about half of the country’s exports. (With files from Reuters and Bloomberg)

content:
Tad DeHaven 11 月 12 日，特朗普总统表示，英伟达“只有一个人”取代黄仁勋。他指的是苹果前首席执行官蒂姆·库克。 11 天后，英伟达宣布黄仁勋复职，特朗普对 CNBC 表示，“我做了这笔交易。”  为什么总统要达成这样的协议？黄在承认与一名涉嫌与中国情报部门有联系的女性有染后辞职。两位英伟达股东敦促董事会对让他回归持开放态度。一名英伟达员工建立了一个网站，人们可以在上面签署一封呼吁他回归的信。股东和员工完全有权向董事们提出自己的理由，而董事们在 11 月 17 日告诉投资者，他们无意恢复黄的职位。英伟达董事会也有充分的理由询问联邦官员对可疑情报行动的了解。根据董事会的声明，政府的回答缓解了他们对国家安全的担忧。他们还会见了黄，并表示他们对他能够领导公司感到满意，尽管他们自己的调查仍在进行中。但特朗普向他们施压，要求他们恢复黄的职位，从而越界了。任何仍然认为让黄回来是一个错误的董事都被迫权衡英伟达违抗总统可能付出的代价。这让人有理由怀疑英伟达董事会恢复黄仁勋的决定是否真的正确。如果董事会的内部调查发现更多涉及黄的令人不安的信息，会发生什么？
特朗普宣称其复职对美国繁荣至关重要，它会不愿意对这位首席执行官采取行动吗？当 CNBC 的萨拉·艾森问特朗普他的底线在哪里时，他回答说：“我是为了国家而这样做。”用特朗普的话说，美国的繁荣取决于黄仁勋掌管英伟达。难怪吉姆·克莱默在同一次电话会议上询问，如果该公司陷入财务困境，华盛顿是否会提供援助。特朗普表示，他认为事情不会发展到这个地步，但他正在回答有关一家上季度盈利 653 亿美元的公司的救助问题。我们已经看到，当华盛顿认定一家公司太重要而不能倒闭时，董事会会发生什么。 2009年，通用汽车依靠联邦救助维持生存，奥巴马政府罢免了首席执行官里克·瓦格纳，并任命了他的继任者弗里茨·亨德森。亨德森后来告诉调查人员，通用汽车的董事认为财政部篡夺了他们选择首席执行官的权力。美国政府已经对英伟达的业务拥有足够的发言权，可以要求削减对中国的某些芯片销售。下次特朗普向黄求助时，他可以提醒黄是谁帮助他重新获得了工作。正如我的同事斯科特·林西科姆 (Scott Lincicome) 今天指出的那样，这种干预的经济成本比周一英伟达股价的上涨更难以看出。以英特尔为例。 2025 年 8 月，特朗普因首席执行官陈立武 (Lip-Bu Tan) 与中国的关系而要求他辞职。
谭匆匆赶到白宫，特朗普说他在那里告诉他，“如果你聪明的话，就把你公司 10% 的股份交给美国。”谭保住了他的工作，联邦政府成为英特尔股东。同月，蒂姆·库克前往白宫寻求苹果的关税豁免。正如斯科特所记录的那样，据报道，特朗普和商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克向库克施压，要求英特尔生产一些苹果芯片。苹果获得了豁免。十个月后，特朗普将他所说的苹果和英特尔之间的交易归功于自己。 “我们是

【原文 English Original】
Tad DeHaven On November 12, President Trump said there was “only one man” to replace Jensen Huang at Nvidia. He meant former Apple CEO Tim Cook. Eleven days later, Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement, and Trump told CNBC , “I made the deal.”  Why was that the president’s deal to make? Huang resigned after acknowledging an affair with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Two Nvidia shareholders urged the board to keep an open mind about bringing him back. An Nvidia employee set up a website where people could sign a letter calling for his return. Shareholders and employees had every right to make their case to the directors, who had told investors on November 17 that they had no intention of reinstating Huang. Nvidia’s board also had good reason to ask federal officials what they knew about the suspected intelligence operation. The government’s answer eased their national security concerns, according to the board’s statement . They also met with Huang and said they were satisfied that he could lead the company, though their own investigation remains open.  But Trump crossed the line by pressuring them to reinstate Huang. Any director who still thought it was a mistake to bring back Huang was forced to weigh what it might cost Nvidia to defy the president. That makes it fair to wonder whether Nvidia’s board was truly kosher with reinstating Huang. What happens if the board’s internal investigation turns up more troubling information involving Huang? Will it be reluctant to act against a CEO whose reinstatement Trump declared essential to American prosperity?  When CNBC’s Sara Eisen asked Trump where he drew the line, he replied, “I’m doing it for the country.” In Trump’s telling , American prosperity depends on having Huang at the helm of Nvidia. Little wonder that Jim Cramer asked on the same call whether Washington would come to the company’s aid if it got into financial trouble. Trump said he didn’t think it would come to that, but here he was fielding a bailout question about a company that earned $65.3 billion last quarter. We’ve seen what happens to a board when Washington decides a company is too important to fail. In 2009, while General Motors depended on a federal bailout to stay afloat, the Obama administration ousted CEO Rick Wagoner and appointed his successor, Fritz Henderson. Henderson later told investigators that GM’s directors felt Treasury had usurped their authority to choose the CEO. The administration already has enough say over Nvidia’s business to claim a cut of certain chip sales to China. And the next time Trump asks Huang for a favor, he can remind him who helped get him his job back. As my colleague Scott Lincicome pointed out today , the economic costs of this kind of interference are harder to see than Monday’s jump in Nvidia’s share price.  Take Intel . In August 2025, Trump called on CEO Lip-Bu Tan to resign over Tan’s ties to China. Tan scurried to the White House, where Trump says he told him , “If you’re smart, give the United States of America 10 percent of your company.” Tan kept his job, and the federal government became an Intel shareholder.  That same month, Tim Cook went to the White House seeking a tariff exemption for Apple. As Scott has documented , Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly pressed Cook to have Intel make some of Apple’s chips. Apple got its exemption. Ten months later, Trump took credit for what he described as a deal between Apple and Intel. “We want capital flowing to companies for commercial reasons,” Scott told the New York Times . Good luck with that when the president is out recruiting customers for a company in the federal portfolio . “Investors have grown accustomed to President Trump influencing the prospects of different companies, whether it’s rare earth metals, energy, and chips,” JoAnne Feeney, a portfolio manager at Advisors Capital Management, told Bloomberg . “It certainly has made investing more complicated because it has to be factored into which stocks you choose to hold. It’s not the way the US capitalistic system is designed.” No, it’s not .  Huang is due to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3 about chip exports. Congress is already asking the administration which officials weighed in with Nvidia’s board and what they said to get Huang reinstated.  But Congress ought to keep Nvidia in mind as it considers the Senate’s defense authorization bill . Section 1051 would let the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital buy stakes in suppliers of critical minerals and other materials while barring its director from taking a board seat or obtaining other voting representation. Trump didn’t need a seat on Nvidia’s board to get its directors on the phone. Now imagine taking that call when the federal government is also one of your largest shareholders.

This is the third of a three-part series on China’s relationship with Europe.   The negative numbers began to cascade across European balance sheets as soon as China entered the World Trade Organization in late 2001.   But the cost-benefit calculations were not equal for all Europeans. Some nations, such as Germany, initially gained from high-value exports and joint ventures. Others, like Greece and Portugal, faced a surge of low-cost Chinese goods and strategic investments by entities linked to the Chinese state.  The Chinese economy was barely one-eighth the size of that of the European Economic Community before the People’s Republic embarked on its policy of “reform and opening up” at the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee in December 1978. By 2025, the relative economic weight of China and the European Union was almost equal. Together they account for about a third of world trade. In 1975, their bilateral trade was worth about €2bn ($2.2bn) annually; 50 years later, it was €2bn a day , according to figures compiled for the Institut Jacques Delors.   By any measure, it should have been a success story. But the two were not playing on the same field. State subsidies in China, ranging from concessionary land deals to direct financial aid and favorable local taxation, handed Chinese firms a competitive advantage which added to their low labor costs. A thicket of protectionist rules and non-tariff barriers to entry frustrated foreign enterprises and channeled investment into joint ventures tied, inevitably, to forced technology transfer.   The EU trade deficits with China climbed remorselessly, from €39.6bn in 2001 to peak at €397bn in 2022 after the Covid-19 pandemic, before settling above €350bn annually. New infrastructure accelerated the flow of exports. While Chinese goods had to be shipped or flown to the United States, they could be loaded onto trains to Europe, cutting the transit time from more than a month to less than two weeks, avoiding bottlenecks and crisis points. Traffic on the railway link multiplied almost tenfold in the last decade.  At the same time, China’s leaders redirected their own investments abroad from buying fixed assets, like ports and factories, into new plants built to get around tariffs on electric vehicles and similar items. The Communist Party encouraged rapid growth in research and development, no longer content to copy and to sell. It meant to originate and to own the value in new products.  China’s patent filings now dwarf those by the EU, its universities regularly outrank their European counterparts, and Chinese academics lead the world in scientific publications. In short, a juggernaut was coming for the workplaces and welfare systems of Europe. The response has been episodic and ineffective.  In 2003, the European Commission declined to recognize China as a market economy, prompting ire in Beijing. The next year, the two made a customs co-operation agreement and pursued “dialogues” on tricky subjects like intellectual property and industrial policy.   A decade later, the EU changed its anti-dumping regulations to stay compliant with its WTO obligations but still refused to define China’s economy as playing by market rules. By then, Xi Jinping was settled in power, having taken all the great offices of the Chinese system between 2012 and 2013. Xi encouraged engagement on big-picture issues like climate change, but his focus on exports and technology acquisition was relentless. Meanwhile, waves of repression inside China created political barriers, notably to a bilateral agreement on investment which foundered amid strident criticism in Europe of the human rights abuses against the Uyghur Muslim minority in the far west of China. Such protests were never likely to move the Chinese leader. They merely encouraged him to grow economic ties with Russia and countries in what China was soon calling the “Global South.” The Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, followed by EU economic sanctions, deepened the dependency between Moscow and Beijing.   Their bilateral trade almost doubled as Russian oil and gas fueled Chinese factories and Chinese-made electric cars poured into the Russian market.  European leaders found that the political climate turned hawkish; Europe found itself caught between trade wars, a new strain of assertiveness in Chinese politics and the search for a balance between co-operation and rivalry, both between China and the West and within the EU. The Chinese decision starting in April 2025 to restrict exports of rare earths, valuable minerals for manufacturing everything from catalytic exhausts to pharmaceuticals, in reprisal for President Donald Trump’s tariffs, shocked business and political elites.  The “second China shock” has hollowed out the German industrial belts, forcing Berlin to move closer to the French preference for tariffs and barriers. By some counts in the German media, the country is losing more than 10,000 industrial jobs a month, fueling support for the right-wing AFD party, while France is struggling with its public debts.  In October, the two nations submerged their differences to write to the European Commission, urging it to use the trade weapon against competitors who exploited state subsidies and undervalued currency to destroy their rivals. There is also talk of diversifying supply chains and a “buy Europe” policy. The letter did not name names, but everyone knew the target was China. The proposed “second strike” capacity aimed at imposing duties on countries that retaliate when the EU imposes trade measures is an escalatory step that has uncomfortable echoes of nuclear deterrence doctrine. In Beijing, the Ministry of Commerce is unsheathing its own weapons and already talks of countries harming themselves by “wrong steps.”   The scene is set for a showdown of some kind. It is a far cry from the hopes of 2001.  Michael Sheridan is a veteran British foreign correspondent and is the author of ‘ The Gate to China ’, an acclaimed history of Hong Kong, and ‘ The Red Emperor: Xi Jinping and His New China ’, which is published by Hachette Books and has been translated into a dozen languages, including Ukrainian, Polish, and Japanese.   Europe’s Edge  is CEPA’s online journal covering critical topics on the foreign policy docket across Europe and North America. title: China warns US against imposing new tariffs
zh_title: 中国警告美国不要征收新关税
summary: 在媒体报道称华盛顿计划宣布对中国和其他国家征收新关税后，北京周三敦促美国“维护贸易关系的稳定发展”。中国外交部发言人郭家坤。资料图：中国外交部。报道称，华盛顿的新征税措施将影响包括中国、欧盟、日本和韩国在内的美国主要贸易伙伴。当被问及华盛顿报道的计划时，中国外交部发言人郭家琨表示：“关税战和贸易战不符合任何人的利益。”
content:
在媒体报道称华盛顿计划宣布对中国和其他国家征收新关税后，北京周三敦促美国“维护贸易关系的稳定发展”。中国外交部发言人郭家坤。资料图：中国外交部。报道称，华盛顿的新征税措施将影响包括中国、欧盟、日本和韩国在内的美国主要贸易伙伴。当被问及华盛顿报道的计划时，中国外交部发言人郭家琨表示：“关税战和贸易战不符合任何人的利益。”他在例行新闻发布会上表示，世界两大经济体于 2025 年在贸易战中达成了脆弱的休战协议，“应该通过协商解决相关问题”。他补充说，对产能过剩的指控——亏损大规模生产以涌入海外市场并削弱当地竞争对手——是“虚假前提”和“政治操纵的借口”。中美双方应共同努力，切实落实两国元首达成的重要共识，维护中美经贸关系稳定发展。唐纳德·特朗普总统长期以来一直批评中国对美国不断扩大的贸易顺差，他将其归咎于当地制造业实力和就业机会的下降。
去年开始第二任期后，特朗普对中国商品征收新关税，引发了与北京针锋相对的升级，关税一度飙升至 145%。美国总统唐纳德·特朗普和中国国家主席习近平于 2026 年 11 月 19 日星期四在中国深圳举行的亚太经合组织 (APEC) 会议上。照片：白宫/Daniel Torok。特朗普和中国国家主席习近平于 2025 年 10 月达成的贸易停火协议将于 1 月到期，此前该协议于 9 月同意延长两个月。两人上周在中国南方深圳举行的 APEC 峰会上会面，并将于 12 月在美国举行的 G20 峰会上再次见面。在与俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京举行历史性三边会谈之前，习近平在亚太经合组织会议上赞扬了中国与美国“稳定和改善”的关系。中国领导人还表示，中国应该在人工智能领域开展合作，让技术“处于人的控制之下”，防范安全风险。

【原文 English Original】
Beijing urged the United States on Wednesday to “uphold the stable development” of trade relations, after media reports said Washington was planning to announce new tariffs on China and other countries. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun. File Photo: China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The reports said that Washington’s new levies would affect major US trading partners including China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea. “Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone’s interest,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, when asked about Washington’s reported plans. He told a regular briefing that the world’s two top economies, which in 2025 agreed a tenuous truce in their trade war, “should resolve relevant issues through consultation”. He added that accusations of overcapacity — mass production at a loss to flood overseas markets and undercut local rivals — was a “false premise” and a “pretext for political manipulation”. “China and the United States should work together to effectively implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and uphold the stable development of China-US economic and trade relations,” he said. President Donald Trump has long criticised China’s yawning trade surplus with the United States, which he has blamed for a decline in local manufacturing prowess and jobs. After starting a second term in office last year, Trump imposed new tariffs on Chinese goods, kicking off a tit-for-tat escalation with Beijing that at one point saw duties soar as high as 145 percent. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen, China on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Photo: White House/Daniel Torok. The trade ceasefire struck by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in October 2025 is due to expire in January, after a two-month extension was agreed in September. The two men met last week at an APEC summit in Shenzhen in southern China and are due to see each other again in December at a G20 summit in the United States. During their meeting at APEC, which came just before a historic trilateral with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Xi hailed China’s “stable and improved” ties with the United States. The Chinese leader also said that his country should cooperate in the field of artificial intelligence, keeping the technology “under human control” and guarding against safety risks.

title: Tai Po fire: Hong Kong security chief defends police enquiries surrounding memorial events citing ‘sedition’ risks
zh_title: 大埔火灾：香港保安局局长为警方围绕纪念活动的调查辩护，称存在“煽动叛乱”风险
summary: 香港保安局局长邓克里斯在周四大埔致命火灾周年纪念活动之前为警方的调查进行了辩护，称这些调查对于进行风险评估和防止“煽动”行为是必要的。保安局局长邓克里斯。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 2025年11月26日，大埔宏福苑七栋住宅楼发生大火，造成168人死亡、数千人流离失所。成立了一个由大法官洛克 (David Lok) 担任主席的独立委员会来调查起火原因。唐周三在广播节目中表示，当局采取“
content:
香港保安局局长邓克里斯在周四大埔致命火灾周年纪念活动之前为警方的调查进行了辩护，称这些调查对于进行风险评估和防止“煽动”行为是必要的。保安局局长邓克里斯。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 2025年11月26日，大埔宏福苑七栋住宅楼发生大火，造成168人死亡、数千人流离失所。成立了一个由大法官洛克 (David Lok) 担任主席的独立委员会来调查起火原因。唐周三在广播节目中表示，当局采取“基于风险的方法”，并负责评估任何纪念活动的范围，包括其形式、预期参与人数和潜在风险。唐发表此番言论之前，警方于本月早些时候对两座天主教堂进行了调查，这两座教堂正计划为这场致命火灾举行追悼会。大埔圣母无原罪圣心堂后来将周年纪念弥撒改为为“过去一年去世的兄弟姐妹”举行的一般仪式，教区居民和参加者表示此举是迫于当局压力的结果。唐周三表示，当局必须防止恶意行为者“利用特殊日期进行煽动行为”。致命火灾后的宏福苑，2026 年 4 月 23 日。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。
“仍然有人说政府收购宏福苑是为了高价出售土地。这显然是错误的，政府已经明确表示该土地将用于社会设施，”邓用粤语说。 “是否有人继续以这种方式煽动社会不稳定？我们有责任（知道），”他补充道。唐说，只要合法，纪念活动都是允许的，但他警告说，可能有人别有用心地试图“劫持”此类活动。他没有具体说明是谁。当被问及警方是否会敦促高风险活动的组织者取消活动时，唐表示，当局只会提醒他们潜在的风险，例如网上出现任何暗示可能造成干扰的评论。他说，当局没有统计有多少活动被取消，并补充说，这取决于组织者的决定。上周，一场旨在分享火灾中移民幸存者故事的新书发布会在原定举行前一天被取消。

【原文 English Original】
Hong Kong’s security chief Chris Tang has defended police enquiries ahead of memorial events marking Thursday’s anniversary of the deadly Tai Po fire , calling them necessary to conduct risk assessments and prevent “seditious” acts. Secretary for Security Chris Tang. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. On November 26, 2025, a blaze engulfed seven residential towers at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po, killing 168 people and displacing thousands. An independent committee chaired by Justice David Lok was set up to examine what caused the fire. Speaking on a radio programme on Wednesday, Tang said authorities take a “risk-based approach” and are responsible for assessing the scope of any memorial event, including its format, expected turnout and potential risks. Tang’s remarks followed police enquiries earlier this month into two Catholic churches planning memorial services for the deadly blaze. One church, the Immaculate Heart of Mary Church in Tai Po , has since replaced the anniversary mass with a general service for “the brothers and sisters who died in the past year,” with parishioners and attendees suggesting that the move was the result of pressure from the authorities. Risk of ‘seditious acts’ Tang said on Wednesday that authorities had to prevent malicious actors from “using the special date to conduct seditious acts.” Wang Fuk Court after deadly fire, April 23, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. “Some people are still saying that the government acquired Wang Fuk Court to sell the land at a high price. This is clearly false and the government has made it very clear that the land will be used for social facilities,” Tang said in Cantonese. “Is anyone continuing to incite social instability in this way? It is our responsibility [to know],” he added. Tang said memorial events are permitted as long as they are lawful, but warned that there might be people who seek to “hijack” such events with ulterior motives. He did not specify who. Asked whether police would urge organisers of high-risk events to call them off, Tang said authorities would only remind them of potential risks, such as the emergence of any online comments suggesting possible disruption. He said authorities do not keep a tally of how many events have been called off, adding that it is up to organisers to decide. Last week, a book launch set to share stories from migrant survivors of the fire was called off, a day before it was scheduled to take place.

title: Hang Seng Index closes below 22,000 points on chipmaker losses
zh_title: 芯片制造商亏损 恒生指数收跌22,000点
summary: 芯片制造商亏损导致恒生指数收跌22,000点|中国劳工布告栏 星期三, 2026 年 11 月 25 日 · 香港 香港及中国劳工英文新闻 芯片制造商亏损，恒生指数收盘跌破 22,000 点 受芯片制造商拖累，港股周三收盘跌破 22,000 点。恒生指数下跌1.14%，华虹宏力半导体下跌17.3%。内地指数亦下跌。据《标准报》报道，在芯片制造商亏损的带动下，香港股市周三未能维持早盘涨幅，收盘跌破 22,000 点大关。
content:
芯片制造商亏损导致恒生指数收跌22,000点|中国劳工公告栏
星期三, 25 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港和中国劳工新闻（英文）
芯片制造商亏损 恒生指数收跌22,000点
周三港股受芯片制造商拖累，收跌22,000点下方。恒生指数下跌1.14%，华虹宏力半导体下跌17.3%。内地指数亦下跌。
据《标准报》报道，在芯片制造商亏损的带动下，香港股市周三未能维持早盘涨幅，收盘跌破 22,000 点大关。
恒生指数跌 253 点，跌幅 1.14%，报 21,966 点，全日成交额 2,299 亿港元。恒生科技指数下跌 2.56%，至 3,378 点。
芯片制造商拖累了市场。蓝筹股中，华虹宏力(1347)跌幅最大，跌17.3%；中芯国际(0981)跌7.6%。
值得注意的是，宁德时代（3750）和联想（0992）跌幅在恒指成分股中位列第二和第三，分别下跌12.2%和11.1%。科技股阿里巴巴(9988)和腾讯(0700)均下跌约1.2%。 Z.AI（2513）和MiniMax（0100）也继续下跌，分别下跌15%和13.8%。
相反，京东(9618)收盘升3.4%，而理想汽车(2015)则在公布最新业绩前收升2.5%。
内地方面，上证综指跌2.03%至3,476点，深证成指跌3.24%至10,086点。

Hang Seng Index closes below 22,000 points on chipmaker losses | China Labour Bulletin Board
Wednesday, 25 Nov 2026 · Hong Kong Hong Kong and China labour news in English
Hang Seng Index closes below 22,000 points on chipmaker losses
Hong Kong stocks ended Wednesday below 22,000 points, dragged down by chipmakers. The Hang Seng Index fell 1.14 per cent, with Hua Hong Grace Semiconductor plunging 17.3 per cent. Mainland indices also declined.
Hong Kong stocks failed to sustain early gains and closed below the 22,000-point mark on Wednesday, led by chipmakers' losses, according to The Standard.
The benchmark Hang Seng Index fell 253 points, or 1.14 per cent, to 21,966 points, with a full-day turnover of HK$229.9 billion. The Hang Seng Tech Index decreased 2.56 per cent to 3,378 points.
Chipmakers weighted down the market. Hua Hong Grace Semiconductor (1347) plummeted the most among blue chips, down 17.3 per cent, while Semiconductor Manufacturing International Cooperation (0981) fell 7.6 per cent.
Notably, CATL (3750) and Lenovo (0992) recorded the second- and third-largest losses among HSI constituents, slipping 12.2 per cent and 11.1 per cent, respectively. Tech heavyweights Alibaba (9988) and Tencent (0700) both dropped around 1.2 per cent. Z.AI (2513) and MiniMax (0100) also continued to decline, diving 15 per cent and 13.8 per cent.
Conversely, JD.com (9618) climbed 3.4 per cent at the close, while Li Auto (2015) ended 2.5 per cent higher before releasing the latest results.
In the mainland, the Shanghai Stock Exchange Composite Index went down 2.03 per cent to 3,476 points, while the Shenzhen Stock Exchange Component Index retreated 3.24 per cent to 10,086 points.

title: 中共介選再出招 冒名台灣學者打造假輿論

content:
標籤: 中共, 介選, WeTalk, 自由衛隊, 九合一選舉
【大紀元2026年11月25日訊】（大紀元記者吳旻洲台灣台北報導）九合一選舉前夕，安全單位再度發現中共對台介選事件。中共設立名為「WeTalk」、「自由衛隊」等內容農場網站，以程式大量轉載台灣傾共媒體新聞，藉由臉書粉專傳回台灣，並冒用數十位台灣學者專家名義，撰寫呼應中共敘事的專欄，學者發現後即時通報，提醒國人不要受騙上當。
安全單位發現，「WeTalk」與「自由衛隊」由相同團隊管理，追溯發文來源，發現來自「中國聯通北京省網」的IP位址；超過4000則文章中，超過90%使用程式自動化轉載國內特定媒體的新聞，並偽冒高達數十位包含台大、政大、台師大等校的學者教授撰寫專欄文章，配合中國敘事攻擊台灣政府。
安全單位表示，今年4月「鄭習會」後一星期內，中共在臉書設立「嗆爆蛙」等多個粉專，以新聞媒體自居，在共軍「海峽雷霆-2025A」演習後一個多月開始積極運作，包含嘲諷海鯤號、教召、海馬士，質疑台灣打不了仗。
不僅如此，還透過AI漫畫等方式嘲諷賴清德與民進黨政府；影射美國隨時放棄台灣，甚至將台灣拿來交易；9月後則將火力轉向攻擊沈伯洋，並透過空白網軍帳號反覆替這些粉專按讚、灌留言等方式放大聲量與觸及。
安全單位分析後發現，這些粉專原先只是配合中共內容農場文章擴散轉發，後來將自己包裝為新聞頻道，台灣學者則被隨機拿來為這些文章冒名背書，以所謂「專家約稿」的方式被冒用，形成擅長財經的學者撰寫政治、專長歐陸哲學的老師評論台灣民生、專攻勞動經濟的教授評論食安議題的荒謬景象。
調查過程中發現，這些農場與粉專發文時間集中在平日上午10、11點與下午，中午幾乎停發，週末也只占5.5%，作息如同上班族照班表排班。
美國媒體路透社日前報導，除了內容農場與臉書粉專，安全單位近期發現一批在過去4個月內批次建立，且多數被識別為來自中國，將近2700個問題帳號，隨時有可能被用來影響選舉，並通報Meta處理。
Meta發言人則回應說，該公司已移除這些帳號，其中許多帳號早已被系統停用，均屬低品質的假帳號 ，沒有任何帳號曾發布公民議題相關內容，且多數帳號並無任何追蹤者。
由於近期持續傳出中共藉由各式粉專、內容農場蒐集國人個資，傳送不實介選資訊，試圖介入我國選舉，甚至隔海指揮議員候選人拍攝民眾面容照片，提供中共國網軍製作更逼真的假帳號。
陸委會副主委沈有忠日前警告，中共的AI技術持續進步，高科技手法也比過去更加具體、細緻，面對中共對台灣民主政治的滲透，呼籲國人提高警覺，面對不實訊息及威逼利誘都要謹慎防範。
如果您有新聞線索或資料給大紀元，請進入安全投稿爆料平台。

title: Why the Shenzhen Summit Does Not Mark a New “Tripolar” Order

为什么深圳峰会没有标志着新的“三极”秩序 bbert@hudson.org 星期二, 11/24/2026 - 13:21 SVG 评论 2026 年 11 月 23 日 国家利益 为什么深圳峰会没有标志着新的“三极”秩序 虽然美国、中国和俄罗斯超越了其他大国，但它们缺乏将世界划分为势力范围的能力。齐波拉·弗里德 (Tsiporah Fried) 客座高级研究员 齐波拉·弗里德 (Tsiporah Fried) 评论说明文字 中国国家主席习近平、美国总统唐纳德·特朗普和俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京于 2026 年 11 月 19 日在中国深圳出席亚太经合组织 (APEC) 领导人非正式会议。 (Getty Images) 切换目录 目录 内容 分享到 Twitter Twitter 分享到 Facebook Facebook 分享到 LinkedIn LinkedIn 分享到电子邮件 电子邮件 打印 打印 唐纳德·特朗普、习近平之后数小时，弗拉基米尔·普京在深圳发表和平宣言，俄罗斯导弹和无人机袭击了乌克兰的电力基础设施。特朗普周五在华盛顿发表讲话，讨论了他与普京的单独会谈，并表示他相信俄罗斯总统希望结束战争。当被问及乌克兰在这样的解决方案中可以期待什么安全保障时，他回答说：“我不想谈论安全保障，因为我们必须首先达成协议。”然而，对于基辅来说，这一序列提出了一个更根本的问题：乌克兰总统如何能在不保证俄罗斯不会重新点燃冲突的情况下同意结束战争？
这种对比体现了深圳峰会的承诺和假设。三个核大国的领导人有充分的理由进行直接对话，因为每个国家都有能力威胁其他国家的安全。但这并不是三个平等权力的关系。俄罗斯对中国的依赖日益加深，同时其核地位和军事能力也持续存在。三方会议的意义不在于三位领导人达成的共识，而在于会议召开的事实。其象征意义很大，但其实质性成果似乎有限。联合声明没有做出具体承诺，没有解决任何根本冲突，也没有定义谈判框架。尽管如此，它对于为三个大国之间的对话提供直接的政治表达可能具有价值。这种对话是否能产生比外交象征意义更多的东西仍然是一个悬而未决的问题。阅读《国家利益》。喜欢这个分析吗？订阅哈德森的时事通讯，了解我们的最新内容。电子邮件 查看更多订阅选项 外交政策 国际组织

Why the Shenzhen Summit Does Not Mark a New “Tripolar” Order bbert@hudson.org Tue, 11/24/2026 - 13:21 SVG Commentary Nov 23, 2026 The National Interest Why the Shenzhen Summit Does Not Mark a New “Tripolar” Order While the United States, China, and Russia outclass other powers, they lack the reach to divide the world into spheres of influence.   Tsiporah Fried Visiting Senior Fellow Tsiporah Fried Commentary Caption Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin attend a meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders in Shenzhen, China, on November 19, 2026. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents Share to Twitter Twitter Share to Facebook Facebook Share to LinkedIn LinkedIn Share to E-mail E-mail Print Print Hours after Donald Trump , Xi Jinping , and Vladimir Putin issued their Declaration toward Peace in Shenzhen, Russian missiles and drones struck Ukraine ’s electricity infrastructure . Speaking in Washington on Friday, Trump discussed his separate talks with Putin and said he believed the Russian president wanted to end the war. Asked what security guarantees Ukraine could expect in such a settlement, he replied : “I don’t want to talk about security guarantees because we got to get a deal first.” For Kyiv, however, the sequence raises a more fundamental question: how can a Ukrainian president agree to end a war without some guarantees that Russia won’t reignite the conflict? That contrast captures both the promise and the presumption of the Shenzhen Summit . The leaders of the three nuclear powers have compelling reasons to talk directly since each possesses the capacity to threaten the security of the others. Yet this is not a relationship of three equal powers. Russia’s growing dependence on China sits alongside its continued nuclear status and military capacity. The significance of the trilateral meeting lies less in what the three leaders agreed on than in the fact that it took place at all.  Its symbolism is considerable, but its substantive outcome appears limited. The joint declaration establishes no specific commitments, resolves none of the underlying conflicts, and defines no negotiating framework. It may nevertheless have value in giving direct political expression to dialogue among the three powers. Whether that dialogue can produce anything more than diplomatic symbolism remains an open question. Read in The National Interest. Enjoyed this analysis? 黄仁勋本周恢复担任英伟达首席执行官，给震惊华盛顿和硅谷的丑闻增添了另一个转折。风险不仅仅在于股票市场的波动或黄氏事务的色情细节，包括与新加坡公司 Megaspeed 前高管、潜在的中国资产爱丽丝·黄 (Alice Huang) 的关系。从本质上讲，这起丑闻暴露了比任何个人或公司都重要得多的事情：美国的出口管制政策仍然漏洞百出，因无能和内讧而举步维艰，并且脱离了明确的战略。除非华盛顿解决这个问题，否则美国来之不易的人工智能优势可能会受到损害。
这一出口政策的失败不仅仅是具体缺陷的总和。这源于特朗普政府对中国的更广泛立场。华盛顿在拥抱不受限制的人工智能加速的同时，也对北京采取了更加宽松的立场。这种结合为爆炸性的 Megaspeed 丑闻埋下了伏笔，或许还有其他尚未浮出水面的丑闻。结果，中国已经能够获得数量惊人的先进芯片，从而缩小与美国的人工智能差距，并为其人工智能驱动的军事现代化提供动力。据人工智能研究机构Epoch AI称，中国多达三分之一的人工智能算力可能来自走私芯片。中国顶尖的人工智能模型现在仅落后美国几个月。这一微小的差距反映出中国真正的创新和对丰富能源资源的获取，以及其为规避美国控制而做出的不懈努力。
黄仁勋在唐纳德·特朗普总统的要求下重返英伟达，这表明该公司和白宫似乎对阻止中国强大的人工智能芯片完全不感兴趣。相反，国会将负责确保美国利用其计算优势并保持其人工智能优势。中期选举和两党对 Megaspeed 灾难的担忧日益加剧，为国会提供了纠正方向的新动力。其近期议程应包括关闭

How China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S. National Security—and How Congress Can Close It

The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia this week added another twist to a scandal that has transfixed Washington and Silicon Valley. The stakes go beyond the swings of the stock market or the salacious details about Huang’s affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed and a potential Chinese asset. At its core, the scandal has exposed something that matters far more than any one man or company: American export-control policy remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy. Unless Washington fixes this, it risks imperiling the United States’ hard-won advantage in artificial intelligence.
This export policy failure is more than the sum of specific deficiencies. It stems from the Trump administration’s broader posture on China. Washington has embraced unfettered AI acceleration at the same time as it has struck a more accommodating stance toward Beijing. That combination set the stage for the explosive Megaspeed scandal—and perhaps others that have yet to emerge. As a result, China has been able to access an alarming number of advanced chips that have enabled it to narrow the AI gap with the United States and power its AI-driven military modernization. According to the AI research institute Epoch AI, up to a third of China’s AI computing power may come from smuggled chips. China’s top AI models are now just months behind the U.S. frontier. The narrow gap reflects China’s genuine innovation and access to abundant energy resources as well as its relentless efforts to circumvent U.S. controls.
Huang’s return to Nvidia at the behest of President Donald Trump suggests that both the company and the White House seem utterly uninterested in keeping powerful AI chips from China. It will instead fall to Congress to ensure that the United States leverages its compute advantage and maintains its AI edge. The midterm elections and mounting bipartisan concerns over the Megaspeed debacle give Congress new momentum to correct course. Its near-term agenda should include closing known loopholes that played a key role in allowing Megaspeed to supply advanced chips to China, stepping up enforcement of existing controls, and strengthening oversight of the administration’s export-control decisions.
Over the medium term, Congress must also tackle the broader question of how to balance the strategic benefits of exporting U.S. technology to build the world’s AI infrastructure with robust controls to prevent its leakage to China. The long-standing debate over which American AI chips and capabilities Washington should permit to diffuse globally and under what conditions has finally boiled over into the mainstream—and, in a perverse way, the national security community can thank Alice Huang for forcing the issue.
The issue before Congress, however, is much broader than addressing the specifics of the Nvidia scandal. Congress must also contend with the underlying impulses driving the administration’s China policy and install guardrails to avoid the erosion of U.S. export controls. This means that after Congress passes near-term bills to mop up the Megaspeed mess, it must then take the reins on setting long-term export-control strategy.
Congress cannot stand by idly as AI blazes forward. OpenAI’s top model can now perform professional tasks as well as or better than humans 85 percent of the time, up from just 14 percent in 2024. The time an AI model can independently work on a task is doubling every four months. Last week, a researcher at Anthropic announced that AI helped him untangle the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous problems in pure mathematics.
As capabilities have grown, so have risks. Frontier models can now complete simulated cyberattacks on networks on their own, and hackers are using AI models to partially automate their attacks. In the July incident involving the AI platform Hugging Face, rogue AI agents escaped their testing environment and plotted to evade human oversight, underscoring the difficulty of aligning model behavior with human intent. The growing power of AI and the risks from misuse or loss of control make U.S. leadership a national security imperative.
At its core, the U.S.-Chinese AI competition boils down to which country can deploy the best chips in the highest quantities to train and adopt advanced AI models. The Biden administration’s controls slowed Chinese AI developers by leaving them with fewer, worse chips. Nvidia’s top Blackwell chips are nearly seven times better than Huawei’s Ascend equivalents. By the end of 2026, Huawei will likely have produced less than four percent of the compute that Nvidia will have over the same time. As the founder and CEO of DeepSeek, one of China’s top AI companies, admitted in 2024, “Our problem has never been money—it’s the embargo on high-end chips.”
To circumvent Biden-era restrictions, elaborate networks for smuggling and transshipment emerged to divert chips to China from other countries that could legally acquire them, and Chinese companies leveraged export-control loopholes to remotely access U.S.-powered compute through data centers abroad. Chinese firms funded companies such as Megaspeed to facilitate these workarounds. Backed by the Chinese tech giant Alibaba, Megaspeed has purchased $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips since 2023, prompting an investigation from the U.S. government. Chinese companies also used a technique known as adversarial distillation—training their models on the outputs of top U.S. models at a fraction of the compute. All of this needlessly shrank the United States’ AI lead over China, even after the imposition of export controls.
Congress must take the reins on setting long-term export-control strategy.
These developments should have spurred the Trump administration to better resource, enforce, and update the export controls when it came into office. It did the opposite. In May 2025, the administration suspended the Biden administration’s AI Diffusion Rule, which had established rules for which countries could access advanced chips and in what quantities. Then, after initially prohibiting sales to China of Nvidia’s H20 chip, which was custom-built as a less powerful product for the Chinese market, the Trump administration reversed course in December 2025 and greenlighted the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chip. Although the H200 is two generations behind top U.S. chips, it remains superior to anything China can produce. An investigation from the House Foreign Affairs Committee in November revealed that between December 2025 and May 2026, the Trump administration approved the sale of more than 800,000 of Nvidia’s H200 chips and AMD’s MI325X equivalent, including to companies that the Pentagon has designated as linked to the Chinese military. This week, under pressure from Congress, the administration added Megaspeed to the entity list, which blocks those listed from buying U.S. products without a license—but before that, the administration had not added a single new individual or business to the list in 2026.
This regulatory vacuum and policy incoherence created the perfect conditions for Megaspeed. The Singaporean firm at the center of the Nvidia scandal seems tailor-made to operate in the seams of U.S. export controls. In 2024, the Commerce Department initiated a formal investigation of the company, which could have led to sanctions such as being placed on the entity list. But the Trump administration dragged its feet in pursuing the investigation. In the meantime, Megaspeed stocked Southeast Asian data centers with thousands of U.S. chips, enabling remote access for Chinese firms. This remote access loophole in U.S. export controls was a well-known and increasingly popular workaround for China-linked firms, but the Trump administration left it open for nearly two years and closed it only last week amid pressure from the Nvidia scandal. Regardless of the Megaspeed specifics, the net result of the Trump administration’s actions and inaction is that China has enjoyed access to far more computing power than it should have during a vital period of the AI competition.
The administration’s long-awaited closure of the remote access loophole is a welcome step. The rule requires foreign data centers to secure a license before offering significant computing power to China-based customers. It also requires a license to export advanced chips to places that could facilitate remote access and chip diversion, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. This rule will make it harder for firms such as Megaspeed to import chips in the first place, or to use them to serve China-based customers. But the rule will be difficult to enforce because the U.S. Commerce Department does not have the legal authority under export controls to directly regulate services such as cloud computing. More important, the administration’s lax enforcement of past controls—and internal divisions over the new ones—raise serious questions about its willingness to follow through. Huang’s reinstatement as CEO, with Trump’s backing, will make it harder to vigorously enforce these new controls and move toward a tougher posture on China.
Since Congress cannot rely on the administration to fix export controls and protect the United States’ AI lead, lawmakers should urgently advance bipartisan measures to address the underlying conditions that gave rise to entities such as Megaspeed. As a starting point, Congress should pass the Remote Access Security Act, which would give the administration clear legal authority for controlling remote access to data centers powered by U.S. compute. While implementation will require close congressional oversight, getting the right legal structure in place is an important first step. Next, it should work with industry and technical experts to fund and fast-track “on-chip” technologies—basically, features that can verify a chip’s location and counter smuggling and diversion. Beyond sorting out the technical feasibilities, Congress will need to work with industry to understand the implications of on-chip security mechanisms for global competitiveness and the potential surveillance risks should China develop similar controls since it produces much of the world’s legacy chips.
Along with these technical fixes, Congress should seize on the Megaspeed scandal to strengthen oversight. The AI Overwatch Act, which may be included in the annual defense bill, would codify existing export controls on advanced chips into law, preventing the current or a future administration from reversing them. It would also empower Congress to review and block advanced chips sales to U.S. adversaries. Congress can go even further by establishing a new investigative committee or inspector general to strengthen oversight of sensitive chip export-control policies. Together, these actions would go a long way toward combating the circumvention that let firms such as Megaspeed thrive.
Trump has emphasized summitry optics over pushing China on any sensitive issues.
At the same time, closing loopholes and codifying rules is insufficient to fix the underlying issues that led to the Megaspeed scandal in the first place. This mess is directly downstream from Trump’s dovish shift on China that has seen the administration take a softer line on Beijing just as the AI race accelerated. The administration’s own overreach forced Washington into a conciliatory posture. Administration officials failed to realize that China had learned its lesson from the first Trump administration’s trade wars and was poised to retaliate hard in the second term. After China responded to Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and export controls with its own punishing controls on rare earths, the Trump administration found its way into a vaguely defined and fragile truce. This has severely constrained U.S. policymaking, including related to compute controls.
Indeed, Trump became an easy sell for advocates of aggressive AI promotion such as Jensen Huang. This camp argues that U.S. leadership in the global AI race requires pushing American AI technologies to as many parts of the globe as possible—including China. They claim that keeping China “addicted” to the U.S. AI stack gives Washington leverage and outweighs the national security concerns that could come with helping China improve its AI capabilities. Huang even pushed demonstrably false narratives that China’s military was not interested in Nvidia’s chips and labeled his critics as “unpatriotic” for not wanting U.S. chips spread as far and wide as possible and therefore depriving American tech firms of global market share.
Trump, who was interested in stabilizing the relationship with China and prioritizing near-term, transactional victories on trade, bought it. He also broke with decades of U.S. foreign policy precedent to negotiate export controls with China. In a series of “do nothing” leader-level meetings since, the president has emphasized summitry optics over pushing China on any sensitive issues. And Huang’s restoration at Nvidia ensures that the president’s worst impulses on China will continue to be egged on by his favored tech CEO, to the detriment of U.S. national security.
A core part of Congress’s longer-term agenda should be outlining the basic principles to determine who can import or remotely access advanced AI chips and under what conditions. Administrations have gone back and forth over this line-drawing exercise. The Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule would have imposed a global licensing regime that controlled not just the export of chips but also the aggregate U.S.-powered compute that any country could receive. Under Trump, only a handful of countries face restrictions. A smarter approach would condition advanced chip sales on the buyer’s ability to protect them from diversion and guard against misuse by malign actors looking to skirt safety and security rules. Allied and partner governments could demonstrate this by developing robust economic security policies to prevent chip diversion or remote access. Foreign companies would have to show strong compliance and security commitments. In practice, this would mean having internal procedures to ensure that chips are not diverted and maintaining cooperation with Commerce Department officials to verify that such procedures were working.
Congress can also help rebuild allies’ confidence in U.S. export-control policy. There was hard-won, if imperfect, progress on allied alignment in key areas of export controls under the Biden administration, notably with the Dutch and the Japanese on controls of semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The painstaking work needed to get allies on board can be agonizingly slow, but once achieved, it is far more likely to endure than if the United States imposes extraterritorial controls over their objections. The MATCH Act, one of the bills revived following the Megaspeed scandal, requires controls on allied-produced tools if Washington is unable to negotiate allied alignment. It is a rather rude approach at a moment when U.S. export controls seem to be on shaky footing, U.S. tariffs against allies have pushed relations to a near breaking point, and allies rightly question whether the United States still views China as a strategic threat. Instead, Congress should support efforts to create durable frameworks for allied alignment, such as economic security agreements in key strategic sectors.
A longer-term agenda must include fixing the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, the main agency responsible for administering and enforcing export controls. The bureau has been gutted by dismissals and low morale during the Trump administration, but it has been underresourced for far longer. Congress should increase funding and require modernization of the bureau’s antiquated IT system. Just as important, Congress needs to help insulate policymaking decisions from corporate influence, and it can help by insisting that future Commerce Department officials commit to independent and risk-based decision-making to earn confirmation.
None of these steps will be easy. The president’s support of Huang’s restoration shows that stock market fluctuations weigh more heavily in his decision-making than national security, and the administration is unlikely to welcome increased congressional oversight. The Constitution gives the executive wide deference on matters of foreign policy and national security. But Congress has a role in ensuring that the president faithfully executes the laws and is supported by the right resources, oversight, and strategic priorities. The United States’ AI lead may hinge on whether it meets the moment.
